news.title: Democrats May Flip Longest-Held GOP Senate Seat for First Time in 107 Years
news.text: Democrats have their eyes on a potential upset in Kansas, where recent polls show the U.S. Senate race in a dead heat and the Cook Political Report rates the contest Lean Republican with roughly four weeks until Election Day. The position is held by Republican incumbent Senator Roger Marshall, a doctor, who is battling Democrat Adam Hamilton for the seat that has been held by the GOP since 1919, the longest ever for any party, High Plains Public Radio says. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Republicans now hold a narrow majority in both the House and Senate. President Donald Trump carried Kansas by double digits over then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election, underscoring the state’s Republican tilt. But Democrats have maintained a foothold in the state, with Laura Kelly in the governor’s mansion even as Republicans hold both U.S. Senate seats. Newsweek reached out to both Marshall and Hamilton's campaigns via email on Monday for comment. What To Know According to recent polling, Hamilton either leads by a very slim margin or the race is statistically tied. However, on prediction market site Kalshi Monday night, Marshall has 66 percent versus Hamilton's 34 percent. According to prediction market site Polymarket, Marshall has 68 percent compared to 33 percent for Hamilton. Cook says Hamilton is running an "increasingly strong race" and has been launching an attack ad against Marshall, an OB-GYN, over billing and collection practices at his office. Marshall has branded the ad targeting his practice a "lie." The forecaster also highlights that agriculture—and economic concerns impacting fertilizer and gas—are major factors in the Sunflower State and the rising prices make the race more competitive. Meanwhile, Marshall has branded Hamilton as a "radical Democrat," adding that "his sermons are identical to the Democratic Party platform." Democrats are hoping to capitalize on Trump's dropping approval ratings in state and national polls as the midterm elections loom. The president's overall approval and ranking on key policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have slipped as households across America are flagging affordability concerns. Robert Y. Shapiro, professor of political science at the School of International and Public Affairs at Columbia, told Newsweek on Monday when asked if Democrats realistically could flip the seat: "If this is a 'Wave' election it can flip. Or even otherwise since Hamilton is a very good moderate Democrat running against a very vulnerable opponent. This would be then a one off election unless this establishes a viable precedent for future Democratic candidates in Kansas. And possibly for Democrats elsewhere." What the Polls Show In a poll by The New York Times and Siena University last month, Marshall had 47 percent of the potential vote compared to 46 percent for Hamilton, and 7 percent of respondents said they did not know. The poll surveyed 605 likely voters from September 22 to September 30 and had a margin of error of 4.6 points. A Trafalgar Group poll shows Hamilton has 44.4 percent of the potential vote compared to 43.5 percent for Marshall, 2 percent for Libertarian Party candidate David C Graham and 10.1 percent are undecided. The poll surveyed 1,095 likely voters across the state from September 29 to October 1 and has a margin of error of 2.9 percent. A Wedgewood Polls survey last month showed Hamilton with 50 percent compared to Marshall's 48 percent and Graham's 2 percent. The poll surveyed 500 likely voters from September 22 to September 24 and had a 4.4 percent margin of error. Breakdown of Hamilton vs. Marshall Hamilton is pastor of the largest United Methodist Church in the country, the Church of the Resurrection. He founded the Kansas City-area church in 1990 at age 25, according to his campaign website. He won the Democratic Senate primary in August and is running on affordability; a theme Democrats across the country are emphasizing. His campaign is focused on bringing down energy, housing and healthcare costs as well as protecting Social Security, agriculture and ending “chaos and corruption” in Washington, D.C., his website says. Meanwhile, Marshall has been in the U.S. Senate since winning his 2020 election. He has been an OB-GYN in the state for 25 years, his campaign website highlights, and calls himself a fifth-generation "farm kid." Trump endorsed Marshall, labeling him a "strong advocate" for the people of Kansas. His campaign website touts bills from agriculture, border security and rural healthcare as a guide for voters to see what policies are important to the Republican. news.title: GOP's Sununu Surges in Bid to Flip Democrat's New Hampshire Senate Seat
news.text: Democrat Chris Pappas' lead appears to be diminishing versus Republican John E. Sununu in the battle for U.S. Senate in New Hampshire, as midterm elections are roughly four weeks away. A new poll released by Rasmussen Reports shows that 49 percent would vote for Pappas versus 44 percent who would pick Sununu. The five-point lead is a notable difference from a poll last month that showed Pappas with an 11-point lead over Sununu, 45 percent to 34 percent. Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen is set to retire in the Granite State, opening the seat for November's general election. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a toss-up. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Republicans hold a narrow majority in both the House and Senate. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won New Hampshire during the 2024 presidential election over President Donald Trump by less than 3 percent. The state has not elected a Republican senator in more than 15 years. Newsweek reached out to both Sununu and Pappas' campaigns via email on Monday for comment. What To Know About the New Poll According to the new poll showing Sununu's gains, 3 percent would pick Constitution Party candidate Edmond Laplante and 4 percent are not sure. Pappas has 89 percent of Democrats' vote, 15 percent of Republicans and 40 percent of non-affiliated voters, the poll shows. Sununu has 84 percent of Republican support, 8 percent of Democrats' and 44 percent of unaffiliated voters. Pappas has a large lead with women, as 53 percent favor him versus 33 percent for Sununu, while 53 percent of men favor the Republican candidate compared to 42 percent for Pappas. The survey shows a sizable advantage for Pappas, 46, among those 65 and older, with 58 percent compared to 39 percent as Sununu, 62, who represented the Granite State in the Senate from 2003 to 2009, is favored by those under 40 years old. The poll was conducted from October 2 to October 4 among 979 likely New Hampshire voters and has a margin of error of 3 percent. News-rating website AllSides rates Rasmussen Reports as "Lean Right," adding in part that sources with that designation "moderately align with conservative, traditional, libertarian, or right-wing thought and/or policy agendas." Craig Agranoff, political professor at Florida Atlantic University, told Newsweek on Monday, "Republicans have an avenue in NH, but it is a narrow one. Sununu cutting a double digit Rasmussen lead down to 5 points fits a race Cook already calls a toss up. The Sununu name, ticket splitting, and outside money give the GOP a real shot in a state that often votes one way for governor and another for Senate. A 5 point deficit with a month left is not a win. It is a live race." Agranoff added, "Holding the Senate is not a NH only story. Republicans need this seat or a similar pickup to offset losses elsewhere. If Sununu keeps closing, it becomes part of the majority math. If the lead holds near five, it is a warning, not a path." What Other Polls Show A recent survey from the University of New Hampshire shows 50 percent would pick Pappas, 42 percent would pick Sununu, 2 percent would pick Laplante, 2 percent would write in another candidate and 4 percent are undecided. The poll was conducted from September 17 to September 21 among 1,418 likely general election voters, with a margin of error of 2.6 percent. In an August survey from the pollster, Sununu was up 45 percent compared to 43 percent for Pappas, 5 percent would have voted for another candidate and 7 percent were undecided. That poll was conducted from August 20 to August 24 among 1,878 likely general election voters, with a margin of error of 2.3 percent. The results for this survey were within the margin of error, making it a statistical tie. A co/efficient poll last month had the race deadlocked between the two at 46 percent, while 9 percent were undecided. Pappas' favorability was 37 percent compared to a 51 percent unfavorable rating and 13 percent had no opinion. Sununu's favorability was 41 percent compared to a 47 percent unfavorable rating and 12 percent had no opinion. The poll was conducted from September 9 to September 11 among 958 likely general election voters in the Granite State and had a margin of error of 3.15 percent. news.title: Obama plans Detroit rally with El-Sayed in tight Senate race
news.text:
Several polls showed Abdul El-Sayed in a close race with former Republican representative Mike Rogers, in one of the midterm's most expensive contests. (EPA Images pic)
MICHIGAN: Former president Barack Obama and president Donald Trump both plan to campaign in Michigan during the coming weeks in a showdown to bolster their candidates, especially in the key Senate race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and opponent Mike Rogers, just ahead of the Nov 3 election.
Obama’s Oct 24 appearance - coming about a month after former vice president Kamala Harris campaigned with El-Sayed - underscores the stakes for Democrats in Michigan, long seen as a must-win for the party if it wants to retake the Senate. 
In addition to El-Sayed, the rally will feature Michigan secretary of state Jocelyn Benson, who is running for governor, according to a statement Monday from the state’s Democratic Party.
Several polls show El-Sayed within the margin of error in his race against former Republican representative Mike Rogers, with the campaign becoming one of the most expensive in this midterm cycle. 
More than US$280 million has been spent on advertising so far, according to AdImpact. 
Democrats need to flip four seats to take a majority in the Senate and while more races nationally have become competitive, holding Michigan following the retirement of Democratic Senator Gary Peters is seen as essential to that effort.
Trump said at the White House on Monday that he will be in Michigan “in about a week and a half.” He was last in the state in July when he held a rally at the General Motors vehicle testing ground in Milford outside Detroit. The president has spent his time campaigning recently in the Republican-led states of Alabama and Oklahoma.
The question for Republicans is whether Trump will help Rogers. The Epic MRA poll said 57% of Michigan voters polled see Trump unfavourably. Governor Gretchen Whitmer fares next worst with a 42% unfavourable rating.
El-Sayed has been working to court Michigan’s Black voters, who largely backed his Democratic opponent during the primary. A recent poll conducted in the state by Epic MRA in late August had El-Sayed leading Rogers among all voters by 47% to 43%. The same poll had 77% of Black voters backing the Democrat.
Obama has kept a relatively low profile in midterm races so far, though he did travel to Texas to support Senate candidate James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate for governor, at a taco restaurant in Austin in May.
news.summary: Barack Obama’s appearance underscores the stakes for Democrats in Michigan, a must-win state if the party wants to retake the Senate.

The FBI under Joe Biden’s administration allegedly monitored Melania and Barron Trump’s travel movements and tapped into future White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles’ cellphone data to help pinpoint the timing of its Mar-a-Lago search for classified and national security documents that Donald Trump was suspected of improperly keeping, RadarOnline.com can reveal. 

The armed feds executed their search on August 8, 2022, at the Palm Beach, Florida, mansion, and the Trump administration has now released a trove of documents related to Operation Plasmic Echo, which revealed bombshell information about the surveillance of Melania and Barron.'Donald Trump’s Legal Defense Team, Journalists And Campaign Advisers' Were Monitored"Already in the crosshairs for spying on Congress, ex-prosecutor Jack Smith and his team monitored the activities of President Donald Trump’s legal defense team, journalists, and campaign advisers using a pen register device that tracked the calls coming to and from his chief of staff Susie Wiles’ phone, according to newly declassified memos that reveal some of the FBI’s invasive tactics used to target Trump," the White House announced in a statement upon the documents' drop on Monday, October 5.

When agents carried out the raid, both Donald and Melania's bedrooms were tossed looking for evidence, along with the 45th president's office. 

The FBI’s alleged surveillance sweep went all the way to Donald himself, with agents painstakingly logging his calls with then-campaign manager Wiles, even flagging the former president’s mysterious "vanity number," a customized phone number that spells out a memorable word.

While the records keep Trump’s personalized digits under wraps, they tracked his calls down to the second. One May 19, 2023, entry coldly clocked: "2:05 pm The FPOTUS Vanity Number called WILES for 16 minutes and 11 seconds."

"Jack Smith’s surveillance operation was a disgraceful abuse of government power," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement about the newly released documents.

She added, "Spying on political opponents is weaponization of law enforcement, plain and simple. Those responsible must be held accountable."

news.title: Trump’s approval hits new low among Hispanic voters ahead of midterms  - St. Vincent Tribune – Daily St
news.text:
A new poll from the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos has found that United States President Donald Trump’s approval rating remains at a record low as the midterm elections approach in November.

The six-day survey, completed on Monday, found that just 32 percent of US voters approve of the job Trump is doing as president.

While that low rate has held steady since September, the latest Reuters-Ipsos poll suggests his support among Latino voters is continuing to slide.

Trump’s approval rating shrunk this month to 24 percent among Hispanic voters, its lowest point in either of his two terms in office.

The Republican leader had previously made substantial inroads with that constituency.

The Pew Research Center estimated that Trump and his Democratic rival, Kamala Harris, were within three percentage points of each other in the 2024 presidential race, earning 48 percent and 51 percent of the Hispanic vote, respectively.

That rate marked a significant jump for Trump over the 2020 election, when he only earned 36 percent of the Hispanic vote.

Experts have credited the boost in Hispanic support with helping Trump win the 2024 race. His 2020 bid, by contrast, ended in defeat to Democrat Joe Biden.

The Monday poll found that Trump’s gains among Hispanics have largely evaporated.

About 52 percent plan to vote for the Democrats in the November midterms, compared to 26 percent for Republicans.

The upcoming midterm is largely viewed as a referendum on Trump’s second term and will decide whether the Republicans maintain their majorities in the US House of Representatives and the Senate.

Democrats have seized on Trump’s low approval ratings, hoping to translate frustration with the president into voter momentum for their party.

A Democratic majority in one or both houses of Congress would place substantial constraints on Trump’s agenda for the remainder of his time in office.

But Trump has also faced rumblings from within his Republican Party as the November 3 midterms approach.

One Republican incumbent, Representative Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, released a campaign advertisement last month that addressed Trump directly, saying, “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”

She cited Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown as a source of tension. “Some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” she said, pointing to the detention and deportation of immigrants with no criminal record.

Experts have also warned that the president’s shrinking popularity, driven in part by concerns about the cost of living and his decision to launch a war on Iran, could weigh down Republican candidates in key races across the country.

Still, Trump has continued to express confidence about the prospects of his Republican Party in the upcoming midterms.

He has also defended his decision to place himself at the centre of the Republican election campaign strategy. Trump recently launched a 32-day blitz of cross-country rallies ahead of the November 3 midterms.

“Just so you understand, they all want me to go,” Trump said, denying that some Republicans would prefer he keep his distance. “They all want me to go campaign.”

news.title: The gap between Americans identifying as Democrats over Republicans hasn’t been this wide since 2009
news.text:
As both parties gear up for the midterm elections, the gap between Americans identifying as Democrats and Republicans has widened by more than 10 percentage points. 

Fifty percent of Americans identified as Democrats or Democratic leaners, according to a new Gallup poll. This is 11 points higher than the 39 percent of Americans who identified as Republicans or Republican leaners in the third quarter of 2026. 

The 11-point lead is the largest quarterly margin Democrats have recorded since the first quarter of 2009, poll aggregator Interactive Polls wrote on X Monday. At the time, former Democratic President Barack Obama had taken office after winning his first election, flipping nine states. 

While the party in power typically loses congressional seats during the midterm elections, new polling shows just how much Democrats are gaining ground in Senate races in five red states just weeks before voters cast their ballots. This means Republicans will have to fight harder to keep seats that would normally be easy to win.

Democrat James Talarico is leading Republican Ken Paxton 51 to 45 percent in Texas, according to New York Times/Siena University polls released Monday. 

Democrat Mary Peltola is beating Republican Dan Sullivan 50 to 43 percent in Alaska and Democrat Sherrod Brown is beating Republican Jon Husted in Ohio 49 to 46 percent, according to the polls. 

Iowa and Kansas are also seeing tight races. Republican Ashley Hinson is leading Josh Turek 48 to 47 percent and Democrat Adam Hamilton and Roger Marshall are tied at 45 percent in Kansas, the polls show. 

The new polling favoring Democrats is a significant shift in public sentiment from when President Donald Trump won the 2024 election. 

After he defeated then-Vice President Kamala Harris, Trump boasted about the “unprecedented and powerful” mandate the American people gave him as the Democratic Party was left to figure out what went wrong. 

Trump had polled higher than Harris on major issues such as immigration and the economy. 

But nearly two years into his second term as president, Trump faces a record-low approval rating amid a costly and unpopular war in Iran and scrutiny over how aggressive federal agents have been in carrying out his massive deportation of illegal immigrants. 

The president has gone as far as to offer Americans a $5,000 “Trump Dividend” if voters help Republicans keep control of Congress, which he first announced during an usual two-day convention in Dallas that he headlined to drum up support for GOP candidates. Critics have accused Trump’s promise of $5,000 checks of amounting to bribery. 

On Sunday, Trump wrote on Truth Social, “The Polls have ALWAYS underestimated MAGA.”
news.summary: The new polling comes as Democrats in red states are putting up a fight against their Republican opponents
news.author: Rachel Dobkin

news.title: 3 takeaways from our new poll of Latino voters: From the Politics Desk
news.text: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Scott Bland breaks down the key numbers to know from our new national poll of the Latino electorate. Plus, Sahil Kapur dives into Democrats’ lingering divisions over transgender issues. — Adam Wollner 3 takeaways from our new poll of Latino voters Analysis by Scott Bland Latino voters’ swing toward President Donald Trump was one of the defining trends of the 2024 election. Their swing back could define the 2026 midterms, too. That’s the broad takeaway from the NBC News/Telemundo poll that came out Sunday, which showed Democrats with a 24-point lead among Latino registered voters on a 2026 ballot test. That’s a double-digit turnaround from the 2024 edition of the survey — and it comes after Republicans in Florida and Texas made big redistricting bets on extending the party’s results in the last election. Here are three big takeaways from the numbers: The economy is the driving factor. Immigration and border security are still important to many Latino voters, but their top issue is the cost of living, and Trump’s inability to follow through on his campaign promise to lower prices is biting his party. Latino voters gave Trump a 4-percentage-point edge over Kamala Harris in 2024 on who they thought would do a better job handling the economy. Today, they give Democrats a 21-point advantage on the same question. That’s a big reason almost a quarter (22%) of Latino Trump voters said they’re not planning to back Republicans in the midterms, with 14% choosing Democrats and 8% undecided from that group. Visceral feelings on immigration. Again, it’s not a leading issue when voters have to rank them, but Latino voters have strong feelings about Trump’s immigration agenda. Two-thirds say his enforcement policies have gone too far. Only 39% approve of his handling of border security and 30% approve on immigration overall. Meanwhile, 31% of Latino voters say they or someone close to them started carrying ID because of concerns about getting swept up by ICE enforcement operations, and 27% say they know someone who has been deported or detained by ICE since Trump’s second term began. There were key differences across gender, region and more. Just like in the overall electorate, Latino women lean more Democratic than Latino men. And while the sample was small, Latino voters from Florida were less likely to back Democrats than Latino voters elsewhere — something to keep in mind on election night, when it would be unwise to expect uniform swings from 2024 across different regions. ➡️ Related read: How the shooting death of a Houston father is igniting Latino politics in Texas, by Natasha Korecki Trump-district Democrats draw blowback from Human Rights Campaign over trans rhetoric By Sahil Kapur The country’s largest LGBTQ rights group is criticizing some Democrats who are adopting what they see as anti-transgender rhetoric in their campaigns, a point of tension as the party wrestles with how to handle the issue heading into the 2026 election. They include Rep. Marcy Kaptur, D-Ohio, who said in a recent ad, “I voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools because parents know what’s best for their kids, and boys should not play in girls’ sports.” They also include Rep. Don Davis, D-N.C., who is similarly running in a red-leaning district that Donald Trump carried in the last election. In a recent ad, Davis cited a North Carolina law that prohibits trans women and girls from playing on female sports teams, saying there are “real concerns about fairness and safety” for “women and girls in sports.” Human Rights Campaign President Kelley Robinson told reporters today that those candidates are “doing too much and getting too little” with their strategies. “You don’t have to sacrifice any member of our community to win in these races, to have a message that resonates with voters,” Robinson said at a breakfast in Washington. “You’ve got Marcy Kaptur, who not only is bad on the message, but she’s also bad on the policy. I mean, she voted for a bill that would have put forced outing in place nationally. A don’t-say-trans bill, too, right? She’s somebody that hasn’t been with us on either of those sides, so she’s not someone that we’re supporting this cycle,” Robinson said. Meanwhile, Robinson praised former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat who is running again for the Senate in Ohio. Brown has sought to reframe the debate, featuring a voter in an ad who says: “With everything going on, that’s what they’re talking about?” “Sherrod Brown, on the other hand, I think, did a great job in his response ad that we worked with him pretty closely on — in stating what the laws are in Ohio now and reaffirming his support from the community and then, most importantly, letting voters talk for themselves,” Robinson said. In light of the criticism, Kaptur campaign spokesperson Kylie Blitzer said in a statement: “Marcy set the record straight for NW Ohio voters on where she stands: giving parents more say in the classroom and ensuring parents, coaches, and local sports associations — not politicians in Washington — set the rules in their communities to ensure girls’ sports stay fair. She is focused on lowering costs and standing up to special interests using their big money and outsized influence to tilt the playing field in their favor.” A Davis spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Meanwhile, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has not advised 2026 candidates to take any particular approach on trans issues, according to a person familiar with the committee’s thinking, who said it is “supportive of each candidate messaging as they see fit” in their districts while simply encouraging them to “explain to voters where they stand.” Where the Human Rights Campaign and the Democrats they are criticizing agree is that the GOP attacks are effective if left unanswered. But they disagree over how to answer them. Robinson argued that the “core failure” of Democrats and Kamala Harris in 2024 was “the lack of a direct response.” She said of 2026: “We’ve given counsel and guidance that’s really very clear. Address the attack head-on, pivot to your values — the things that you want voters to know about.” A Democratic strategist involved in 2026 races said that is one school of thought, which can be effective in message testing. Another school of thought, said the strategist, is to directly confront the attacks and seek distance on the issue in order to “not look like a typical Democrat.” The latter approach “works better as your district gets redder,” said the strategist, who was not authorized to discuss internal machinations on the record. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

news.title: We Have a New Contender for Dumbest Political Move of the Century
news.text:
The list of things going poorly for Donald Trump is long, but high gas prices are arguably at the top. Thanks largely to his war of choice in Iran, the president who pledged “gasoline below $2 a gallon” has instead delivered a national average that currently stands at $4.37. Diesel costs, which recently topped $6 per gallon and are driving up prices for everyone, have especially strained farmers, truckers, and other core Trump constituencies.

Voters seem to have noticed. The New York Times and Siena University, political polling’s most respected dynamic duo, recently surveyed likely voters in five red states where Democrats are putting up a strong showing. In each, voters disliked Trump’s handling of gas prices more than any other issue. The polls also showed Democrats running for Senate and governor tied or leading in four of the five states, including Texas, Ohio, and Alaska.

Gas prices have caused headaches for presidents before, and their spikes and ebbs correlate closely with presidential job approval. That fact seems to have triggered a Trumpian scramble to tame prices before Election Day, while also inviting Iranian counter-efforts to keep them high.

Even presidents have limited means to manipulate gas prices, but that hasn’t stopped this one from trying. Over the summer, after Trump’s ceasefire with Iran collapsed, the U.S. Navy redoubled its efforts to help tankers transit the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for Middle Eastern oil that Iran blockaded. The president has also tugged levers closer to home. To increase supply, he has released millions of barrels from the U.S.’s emergency petroleum stockpile, draining the reserve to its lowest level in 44 years. Last week, his threats to suspend diesel exports to U.S. allies reportedly forced a group of wealthy countries to agree to release 100 million barrels from their own stockpiles. Lowering gas prices may also have motivated a deal Trump announced over the summer that effectively lets the U.S. seize a portion of Venezuela’s oil reserves.

Some of Trump’s efforts seem to be working, at least on the margins. Oil shipments through the strait have risen, nearly reaching their prewar levels last month. Some polls show Trump’s job approval numbers recovering from all-time lows after prices at the pump dropped by a few cents. And given how much attention voters pay to gas, it’s plausible that even small improvements could save vulnerable Republican candidates. Some red states with competitive midterm races have also temporarily reduced gas taxes, including Texas and Ohio.

But in gas prices as in war, the enemy also gets a say (and in this case, Iran gets a say in both). Iranian attacks on shipping have ramped up over the past week. The Houthis, an Iran-aligned Yemeni militia, have started targeting refineries in Saudi Arabia, a U.S. ally that produces about 11 percent of global oil supply. And Trump seems no closer to permanently ending the war, making a sustained drop in gas prices unlikely for now.

It’s a depressing political reality that the clearest driver of Americans’ unhappiness isn’t the Trump family’s naked corruption or immigration agents shooting people in the streets, but rather the cost of refueling one’s car. Yet recent elections have shown just how sensitive voters are to price increases (just ask Joe Biden and Kamala Harris). And after winning the White House back in part over higher prices, Trump’s decision to smash the bright red “make gas more expensive” button may have handed Democrats the biggest electoral gift they could’ve hoped for.

I can’t promise you lower gas prices, but my colleagues have put together some fun evening reads that might at least help lower your blood pressure:

Listen to the pop-country godmother: If you’re enjoying the country-crossover renaissance exemplified by Ella Langley’s chart-topping song “Choosin’ Texas,” you’re in for a treat: Langley’s mentor, Miranda Lambert, has a new album out. Slate music critic Carl Wilson raves that Crisco is a “nostalgic pleasure cruise through pop-country styles of the past.”

Watch an unhinged new thriller: Verity, starring Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson, and Josh Hartnett, brings Colleen Hoover’s most bonkers book to the big screen. Rebecca Onion digs into the movie’s many twists and turns, culminating in “the psychological-thriller equivalent of a plot quadruple axel.”

Remember a beloved Aussie adventurer: Steve Irwin (aka the Crocodile Hunter) charmed viewers with his reptile-wrestling antics and his deep reverence for the natural world. For the 20th anniversary of Irwin’s untimely death, Ivana Rihter reflects on the conservationist’s legacy.

Contemplate a bizarre fashion trend: Why is this Meta executive dressing like he deals weed? Steffi Cao investigates a billionaire’s scruffy makeover, and explores why Silicon Valley’s power players are styling themselves to appear harmless.

And with that, you’ve officially made it through the first day of what promises to be another long news week (aren’t they all, these days?). See you back here tomorrow!
news.summary: Sometimes, Trump’s terrible policies also make for terrible politics.
news.author: Ian Prasad Philbrick

news.title: Obama to appear with El-Sayed in Detroit as he gets more involved in midterms
news.text:
DETROIT -- Former President Barack Obama will campaign alongside Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit later this month, lending his support to the progressive nominee after a bruising Democratic primary exposed divisions within the party.

Obama will appear with El-Sayed at an Oct. 24 rally that will also feature other top Democratic candidates in Michigan, including Jocelyn Benson, the party's nominee for governor. Obama is getting significantly more involved in the midterm elections, with additional campaign stops and advertisements expected to come in the closing weeks, according to plans shared first with The Associated Press.

The Detroit event is a notable show of support for El-Sayed, who defeated moderate Rep. Haley Stevens in an August primary and has since worked to consolidate Democratic support in his race against Republican Mike Rogers. The open seat is expected to be among a handful that will decide which party controls the majority next year. 

Obama taped two dozen ads last week for Democratic candidates for governor and Senate that will be released in the coming days and weeks, in addition to more campaign stops soon to be announced.

He appeared earlier this year in a campaign ad with Iowa Senate candidate Josh Turek and campaigned in Texas with Senate candidate James Talarico and the candidate for governor, Gina Hinojosa. This week, he will headline a Washington fundraiser supporting Democratic Senate candidates.

El-Sayed defeated Stevens by less than a percentage point in a primary that became a national test of the Democratic Party’s ideological direction. El-Sayed drew support from leading progressives, including Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders and Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York. Stevens was backed by Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer.

Some ads that supported Stevens showed Obama praising her, and she outperformed El-Sayed in Wayne County, winning about 51% of the Democratic primary vote compared with 45% for El-Sayed. The county includes Detroit, where more than three-quarters of residents are Black. 

Kamala Harris, the first Black and South Asian person to serve as vice president, campaigned with El-Sayed last month. 

Now the Oct. 24 rally with Obama, the first Black president, could give El-Sayed a boost on the first day of Michigan’s required early in-person voting period. Obama spoke with El-Sayed by phone following his primary victory.

It will also be a boost for the other candidates in what is one of the most consequential elections in recent Michigan history. There are open races for governor, secretary of state and attorney general, in addition to control of the state legislature being at play. 

Benson, who will also appear with Obama, is facing Republican Rep. John James in the race for governor. 

Benson and James are set to debate for the first time on Tuesday, and El-Sayed and Rogers are scheduled to debate for the first time on Oct. 8. 

Obama has been selective in his involvement in the midterms so far, but his planned ramp-up in the final weeks follows a pattern from recent elections. He campaigned in Detroit on Oct. 22 during the 2024 presidential election and was in the city Oct. 29 during the 2022 midterms. 

His campaign appearances can draw large crowds and prominent guests. Rapper Eminem introduced Obama at his Detroit rally in 2024.

This week, he will headline an event with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee that will include a conversation with Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester. That follows a September event with the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.
news.summary: Former President Barack Obama plans to appear with Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit this month
news.author: Joey Cappelletti Associated Press

news.title: Here’s why Maine’s famous election slogan will be disproven in midterms
news.text:
The midterm election is less than a month away. And all signs point to a bloodbath for President Donald Trump and the Republican Party. The generic congressional ballot, which measures whether voters will pick a generic Democrat or Republican for Congress, shows Democrats have a nine-point lead. 

On an individual level, Democrats have wide leads in swing states like Georgia and North Carolina. And Trump’s gamble to replace the genteel Republican incumbent Sen. John Cornyn with MAGA Attorney General Ken Paxton seems to be blowing up in his face, as Democrat James Talarico leads in polling and fundraising. Vice President JD Vance had to be sent to Alaska Monday, which Trump won by 13 points, to campaign for Dan Sullivan. 

Republicans’ resources will now be stretched thin as they have to play defense not only in the traditional swing states, but even in ruby-red states like Kansas, Iowa and Nebraska. But ironically, even if Democrats massacre Republicans at the polls, they might not get their one prized possession: unseating Sen. Susan Collins in Maine.

On Tuesday night, she will square off in a debate against her Democratic opponent, former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson. By all measures, this should be the year that the five-term incumbent Republican goes down. Kamala Harris won Maine by about seven points. 

The state has a Democratic governor and legislature. Earlier this year, an Immigration and Customs officer in Biddeford shot and killed Joan Sebastian Guerrero. Democrats like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have tried to pin the death on Collins since she voted for increased funding for ICE earlier this year, though Collins argues she put in place body cameras for ICE. 

But polling shows Collins is still in the hunt. A CBS poll showed that she is in a dead heat with Jackson. But other polls show a more difficult race for the challenger. And it might mean that Maine does not live up to its politics motto: “As Maine goes, so goes the nation.” 

Two weeks ago, a New York Times/Siena University poll showed Collins with a three-point lead. 

On the surface, it looks fairly easy to blame this on the debacle that was the Democratic Primary, wherein insurgent candidate Graham Platner won before he ultimately dropped out after a report in Politico that he allegedly sexually assaulted an ex-partner, which he denied. The fact Jackson campaigned heavily with Platner when Jackson ran for governor made it fairly easy for Republicans to tie the two together. 

A look under the hood seems to shows that’s only part of the story. Democrats hope to tie Collins, who has portrayed herself as a moderate New England Republican, closer to Trump this cycle, especially after she voted to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court.

But she still enjoys some crossover support. The Times/Siena poll showed that 44 percent of women still support Collins. Compare that with The Times/Siena Michigan’s Senate race, where only 39 percent of women support Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers. The same holds true for The Times/Siena poll in Kansas, where 40 percent of women support incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall. 

Collins also still has support among a significant slice of Democrats, with 13 percent of self-identified Democrats saying if the election were held today, they’d pick Collins. By contrast, in Michigan, 95 percent of Democrats said they would support Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed. The same amount of Democrats in Texas would vote for Talarico.

Collins also leads Jackson 51 percent to 45 percent with voters identified as “other.” In Kansas, Hamilton has 55 percent of voters with that identification. In Michigan, El-Sayed and Rogers are about dead-even with independents, with 46 percent for El-Sayed and 45 percent.

This support can really only come with years of support Collins has cultivated from being a senator since 1996. As chairwoman of the Senate Appropriations Committee, she regularly touts the millions of dollars she brings back to a largely rural state like Maine and the fact she is an independent senator. 

Collins also bolstered her independent image by voting to convict Trump after January 6, opposing the confirmation of Pete Hegseth as Defense secretary, the confirmation of Todd Blanche as attorney general and the passage of the One, Buig Beautiful Bill. The fact that Collins is probably the only Republican who can win that seat is likely why Trump has largely refrained from criticizing her.

And the chances are that Collins might have more support than even the polls are showing. In 2020, a host of polls had Collins down for the count, only for her to shock everyone and win by almost 8.6 points despite Joe Biden winning the state by about 9 points.

There are significant differences between then and now, though. Collins no longer has the cache of being seen as a pro-abortion rights Republican given the Supreme Court’s Dobbs v Jackson decision in 2022 that killed the constitutional right to an abortion. And she’s voted more in line with Trump this go-around. 

Still, if she pulls off a victory, don’t be entirely surprised that she has pulled one last rabbit out of her hat.
news.summary: Susan Collins might be the one Republican who survives a GOP electoral bloodbath, Eric Garcia writes, defying the old saw, 'As goes Maine, so goes the nation'
news.author: Eric Garcia

news.title: Obama to Make Michigan Midterm Push With Abdul El-Sayed Campaign Event
news.text: Former President Barack Obama will campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan's progressive Democratic Senate nominee, at an event in Detroit, as Democrats fight to hold an open seat that could help decide control of the upper chamber. Obama will appear with El-Sayed at an October 24 rally, less than two weeks before Election Day, alongside other top Michigan Democrats, including gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson. The former president is stepping up his role in the midterms, with more campaign stops and ads expected in the closing weeks. "It is my honor and privilege to announce that President Barack Obama is joining us on the trail in Detroit on Saturday, October 24," El-Sayed wrote on X, where he has more than 300,000 followers. The Detroit event is a notable show of support for El-Sayed, who defeated moderate Representative Haley Stevens in an August primary and has since worked to consolidate Democratic support in his race against Republican Mike Rogers. Obama is the latest in a string of high-profile Democrats to join El-Sayed on the campaign trail in recent weeks. Former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned with him last month in Detroit, where the two held a roundtable on Black maternal health. Polls Show a Tight Race in Michigan Obama's rally news comes as recent polls show El-Sayed holding a narrow edge over Rogers, with several surveys putting the race within a few points. A Fox News poll, conducted by Beacon Research and Shaw & Company Research from September 24 to 28, found El-Sayed leading Rogers 50 percent to 49 percent among 1,028 likely voters. Other polls have given El-Sayed more breathing room. news.title: Joe Scarborough rips Trump’s lack of regrets as Americans struggle
news.text:
MS NOW’s Joe Scarborough slammed Donald Trump after the president told reporters he has no regrets about the choices he has made since returning to the White House. On Monday’s “Morning Joe,” Scarborough said Trump’s response, as millions of Americans struggle under his economy, showed he has “no humility.”

During a gaggle with reporters on the White House South Lawn on Sunday, Trump was asked to reflect on his second term so far. The president called it “great,” saying he has delivered “the most productive two years” and claiming to be the “most consequential” president in U.S. history.

https://twitter.com/gardnerakayla/status/2106601887621361815

As Scarborough noted, Trump made those comments as he faces historically low approval ratings. Americans have grown frustrated with his handling of the economy, including his tariffs and the ongoing war with Iran, which has driven energy prices higher.

“No regrets, no humility, no self-awareness at all,” the MS NOW host said of the president.

Scarborough argued that Americans want a president who acknowledges their concerns, not one who boasts about his accomplishments and focuses on vanity projects instead of advancing policies to improve their circumstances.

“I know it sounds crazy, but Americans would rather the president talk about them than keep talking about himself,” Scarborough said. “Almost like they’d rather him talk about gas prices instead of Marie Antoinette ballrooms, diesel prices instead of grand arches that veterans groups are against, and inflation that he’s supposed to know so much about but obviously doesn’t.”

The “Morning Joe” co-host also compared Trump’s unwillingness to acknowledge his administration’s shortcomings with an infamous moment from the 2024 campaign involving former Vice President Kamala Harris. When the co-hosts of ABC’s “The View” asked Harris whether there was anything she would have done differently than then-President Joe Biden over the preceding four years, she said “not a thing” came to mind.

“Donald Trump, meet Kamala Harris,” Scarborough said. “It didn’t really work out well for her, saying that she wouldn’t change anything with Joe Biden’s last three or four years, when inflation had been high. Now you’re saying the same exact thing.”

You can watch Scarborough’s comments in the clip at the top of the page.

news.title: Supreme Court Hears Oral Arguments in a Major Climate Change Case
news.text:
Progressive lawfare aimed at oil and gas companies reached the Supreme Court today in the form of Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County. This is an attempt by Boulder County to sue Exxon and Suncor over the effects of climate change on the county. 

The Supreme Court of Colorado has already sided with the plaintiffs so unless this is overturned by the Supreme Court it will be the start of a nationwide trend attempting to bankrupt oil companies. Today, eight of the Justices heard oral arguments in the case after Justice Alito recused himself last week. The potential implications of this case are tremendous.

The Supreme Court kicks off a new term Monday with a case ostensibly about climate change but with much bigger stakes. The real issue in Suncor Energy v. Boulder County is whether states and localities can turn federalism on its head to dictate policy for the rest of the country...The Supreme Court ruled unanimously in AEP v. Connecticut (2011) that the Clean Air Act pre-empts similar state nuisance claims related to CO2 emissions. But Boulder is trying to evade the Court’s holding by suing oil and gas producers in state courts. Boulder says the companies created a public nuisance and engaged in a “civil conspiracy” by selling products without warning about their climate effect.The Colorado Supreme Court ruled Boulder’s state claims aren’t pre-empted by federal law. The judges reasoned that Boulder’s claims related to the production and marketing of fossil fuels, not their CO2 emissions. This is a semantic distinction without a difference. Under the Colorado court’s ruling, oil and gas companies would have no choice but to cease producing fossil fuels to avoid enormous liability. That’s the goal of the lawsuits, in addition to extracting a big government payday.

It's pretty amazing that this is happening at the same time Democrats and DSA candidates nationwide are running on "affordability" and blaming Trump for the increased price of gasoline. If progressives get their way in this case the outcome will be hundreds of similar cases, each one demanding billions of dollars from oil and gas companies. Those companies only have one way to make up those losses and that's by passing the costs on to consumers. 

In fact, with the legal costs of their operations effectively infinite under this scheme, their only choice would be to shut down operations or face similar claims from thousands of counties, cities and maybe even individuals. After all, if Boulder County can sue for harms, why not Bob Smith?

And if Boulder can sue Suncor and Exxon for actions taken in other states, why not sue individual consumers for owning gas-powered cars? This lack of a limiting principle for such climate change lawsuits came up today in arguments.

Suncor Attorney Kannon Shanmugam is right: Boulder's argument provides NO meaningful limit to the scope of lawsuits against energy companies. Clarence Thomas just exposed Boulder's plaintiff prosecuting its Suncor Energy case. (Boulder wants to sue energy companies for their ostensible impact on the climate.) Thomas got Boulder's attorney to admit that if he prevails, they could just as easily sue local gas stations. Justice Thomas: "If you prevail, is there a limiting principle to whom you can suit?" All that to say, this scheme would be great news for lawyers but the price of gasoline and oil would spike and never return to earth. The price of electricity would also spike as the cost of natural gas would go up sharply as well. So while the left is campaigning hard on gas prices, progressives are also doing their best to make sure they are much higher thanks to this lawfare.

As mentioned above, Justice Alito recused himself but it sounds like Justice Kavanaugh is not going to be a swing vote on this one.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh on the precedents that support Suncor’s arguments: “As I read them together, [these precedents] make crystal clear that interstate air and water pollution are matters for federal law unless Congress specifically preserves state law. Even Chief Justice Roberts sounded pretty solid.

“Presumably if you prevail, the next day, a municipality in every single state will file a lawsuit that will probably copy your pleadings,” said Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. “How would you think that will work out on the ground?”

However, with only eight justices present, the liberals only need to pick up one vote to create a 4-4 tie. A tie would mean that the lower court ruling would stand. In this case that's the Colorado Supreme Court. So the Boulder case would go forward under a tie. Could they swing Justice Barrett? She also didn't seem convinced Boulder had the law on its side.

Luckily, Trump is president and not Kamala Harris, so the federal government is not siding with the plaintiffs here.

The Trump administration had flipped the government’s position in the case, reversing the Biden administration’s view that would have had it supporting Boulder, expressed in a recent similar case from Hawaii. We'll have to wait for some time in 2027 before the court releases its decision on this case. Fingers crossed for a rejection of this lawfare.

The Boulder County Commissioners didn’t negotiate the Paris climate accord, but they are acting as if they should have had a seat at the table. news.title: Obama Takes On MAGA in Must-Win Senate Race
news.text:
Barack Obama is ramping up pressure against Donald Trump in the final stretch of the midterm campaign as GOP fears escalate over the prospect of a “blue wave” in November.

The former president will campaign in Michigan on Oct. 24 alongside Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson, putting him on the ground in the key battleground just as the state’s early in-person voting begins.

As the Daily Beast previously reported, the Democrat stalwart, 65, is set to headline a Senatorial Campaign Committee fundraiser this week, and he has already begun recording campaign ads for Democratic candidates.

Now he’s increasingly taking the show on the road, coinciding with Trump’s own barnstorming blitz before Election Day on Nov. 3.

The Michigan appearance will be particularly notable for El-Sayed, the progressive firebrand who emerged from a bruising Democratic primary and now faces Republican Mike Rogers in a Senate race that could help determine control of Congress.

“It is my honor and privilege to announce that President @BarackObama is joining us on the trail in Detroit on Saturday, October 24,” El-Sayed wrote on social media. “Get. Ready.”

But El-Sayed has emerged as a deeply polarizing figure, both for MAGA world—and his own party. 

Trump and his allies often label him a “communist,” a “hater” of Israel, and attack his ties to controversial far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker.

Backed by figures like Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, El-Sayed’s platforms—including Medicare for All, wealth taxes, and calls to abolish ICE—have also drawn fierce resistance from Republicans and sparked anxiety among centrist Democrats.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris returned to Michigan to campaign with El-Sayed last month, using a roundtable on Black maternal health to frame November’s contest against Rogers as a fight over women’s access to healthcare.

Obama’s return, meanwhile, comes as the GOP’s own campaign strategy increasingly revolves around damage control. 

Trump is planning an aggressive final-month blitz across 17 states and dozens of events, while Republican candidates in several competitive races have sought to distance themselves from the president. 

The president’s tour began in Texas last week, where embattled Senate candidate Ken Paxton is locked in a surprisingly tight race against Democrat James Talarico.

Trump also visited Alabama and Ohio over the weekend, and will head to Nebraska—a state that he won by nearly 20 points in 2024—on Monday.

The president is also offering what critics describe as “bribes for votes,” promising a $5,000 dividend to every adult in America—provided Republicans win both the Senate and the House.

In another contentious move, the 80-year-old also authorized the creation of $20 million worth of taxpayer-funded ads praising him and his presidency, which have run on ABC, NBC, CBS, CNN, MS NOW, Fox News, and Newsmax as the race heats up.

Polls suggested the GOP could lose control of the House in the midterms, due to backlash to Trump’s disastrous policies, his handling of the economy, and his war with Iran.

Losing control of Congress would inevitably stall Trump’s agenda and expose him and his allies to countless congressional investigations.

“Just get out and vote,” Trump begged voters at his Ohio rally on Saturday.

The former president will campaign in Michigan on Oct. 24 alongside Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson, putting him on the ground in the key battleground just as the state’s early in-person voting begins.

news.title: Jeffries says Democrats are poised to win House majority
news.text:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries expressed confidence Sunday that Democrats would gain the majority by winning key swing districts in places such as Iowa, Pennsylvania, Nebraska, New York and Arizona.

But with just 30 days until the election, he also predicted the party would pad its margins by picking up seats in Republican terrain.

“These districts are going to give us the majority, and then on top of it, the fact that we’ve been able to go deeper and deeper into the map will give us the opportunity to grow that majority even bigger,’’ Jeffries told reporters on a press call.

House Democrats currently have 66 districts on their target list; most of them backed Donald Trump in 2024. The party’s bullish outlook is driven by the president’s sinking job approval numbers and historic trends that suggest the party controlling the White House loses seats in midterm elections.

Battleground districts singled out by Jeffries as strong pickup opportunities included Arizona’s 6th, held by Rep. Juan Ciscomani; New York’s 17th, represented by Rep. Mike Lawler; and Iowa’s 1st District, held by Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks. Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales rates the races either as Toss-ups or Tilt Democratic.

A Sept. 24-27 Quinnipiac University poll found Democrats with a 12-point advantage on the generic congressional ballot, which asks respondents whether they plan to vote for the Republican or Democratic candidate for Congress.

Republicans have long dismissed Democrats’ confidence as overblown and have pointed to the GOP’s strong fundraising advantage in the final weeks of the midterm campaign.

Jeffries, however, insisted that Democrats have the resources to remain competitive.

“We’ve raised, as House Democrats, the resources necessary to go on offense while defending our Frontline incumbent members of Congress, many of whom are well ahead of their Republican challengers, and have begun to put those seats out of reach.”

Both Jeffries and his Republican House counterpart, Speaker Mike Johnson, have embarked on an ambitious travel schedule to boost their candidates during the campaign recess.

Johnson was in California last week, raising money and stumping for several GOP candidates, including Rep. David Valadao, a perennial Democratic target, and former Stockton Mayor Kevin Lincoln, who is challenging freshman Democrat Adam Gray in a Central Valley district that Democrats redrew in their favor in response to Republican-led redistricting in Texas.

New congressional maps in several states has reshaped the House battleground this cycle. While most redistricting efforts have been GOP-led, Jeffries suggested Sunday that Republicans may not pick up as many seats as they had initially thought.

“The political conditions in Texas are deteriorating for Republicans by the day,” the New York Democrat said, pointing to Hispanic voters’ drift from the GOP. He also referred to the new Florida map as a “dummymander” that will fall short of GOP expectations.

Jeffries said he was in California over the weekend campaigning with Gray and former state Sen. Richard Pan, who is running against Republican-turned-independent Kevin Kiley, one of CQ Roll Call’s most vulnerable incumbents. Jeffries said he also plans to visit several other states, including New York and New Jersey, as well as the Midwest and perhaps Florida.

The battle for the House, Jeffries said, is “an all-hands on deck effort” for Democrats, noting the contributions of both former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

Trump has also kept up a busy campaign schedule, visiting four states starting Thursday. At a rally Saturday in Vandalia, Ohio – located in the Democrat-targeted 10th District held by Republican Michael R. Turner – the president declared that Republicans will defy expectations come November.

“They’re in for a big surprise,” he told the crowd. “You gotta get out and vote.’’
news.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries expressed confidence Sunday that Democrats would gain the majority by winning key swing districts in places such as Iowa, Pennsylvania, Nebraska, New York and Arizona.

news.title: Map Shows Donald Trump Approval Rating in States Getting Economic Boost
news.text: President Donald Trump’s approval rating is underwater in all eight states identified for major economic investments recently announced by his administration, including Texas, Tennessee and Iowa. The approval rating data is from Civiqs' rolling online tracker, based on 134,051 responses from registered voters collected between January 20, 2025, and October 3, 2026. The states are set to benefit from a series of major investments announced by the Trump administration, including a $200 billion strategic investment package from South Korea and a $15 billion steel project in Iowa. Newsweek contacted the White House for comment on Monday. Key Points Why It Matters Less than a month before the November midterms, Trump’s approval rating is negative even in states where his administration has announced major economic investments. The investment plans are still at varying stages of development, with some projects yet to be finalized, meaning the economic benefits Trump is touting have yet to materialize. While presidential approval ratings are not a direct measure of how voters will cast their ballots, they offer a snapshot of the political climate heading into the midterms. For Republicans competing in closely watched races, Trump’s standing in their states could shape how they campaign and how closely they align themselves with the president. Alaska Trump’s approval rating is underwater in Alaska, despite the state being set to benefit from a major energy investment announced by the administration. Civiqs shows 54 percent of Alaska voters disapprove of his job performance, compared with 39 percent who approve. This gives him a net rating of minus 15. Trump carried Alaska by 13 points in the 2024 presidential election, but his net approval rating has consistently remained negative in the state since last September. The president announced plans for South Korea to invest $54 billion in an LNG project in Alaska, along with billions more in energy investments. However, the plan’s future was thrown into uncertainty after Seoul said it had not committed to the Alaska project. Trump defended the announcement on Friday, saying he had not “jumped the gun” and that if South Korea did not want to participate, he would “just charge them more,” referring to U.S. tariffs on South Korean goods. Iowa Trump’s approval rating is also negative in Iowa, where a $15 billion steel plant has been announced as part of a major new investment. According to Civiqs, 55 percent of Iowa voters disapprove of Trump's job performance, compared with 36 percent approving, giving him a net rating of minus 19. Trump announced last week that the Minnesota-based Mesabi Metallics will build what is expected to become the largest steel plant in U.S. history in Iowa. The project is expected to create 1,750 permanent jobs in Iowa, a White House official said, per CBS News. Trump won Iowa by more than 13 points in 2024, but his approval rating in the state has been underwater since May of last year. Minnesota Trump’s approval rating is particularly weak in Minnesota, which is set to supply the iron ore for the major new steel plant planned in neighboring Iowa. According to Civiqs, 64 percent of Minnesota voters disapprove of Trump's job performance, compared with 28 percent who approve, giving him a net rating of minus 35. Trump lost Minnesota to Kamala Harris in 2024, and his approval rating has remained negative in the state throughout his second term, according to Civiqs. An Iowa steel plant announced last week that it will use iron ore from a new mine in Nashwauk, Minnesota, which will be the state’s first new iron ore mine in 50 years. The project is expected to provide about 350 jobs in Minnesota’s Iron Range, Mesabi Metallics said. Texas Trump’s approval rating is also underwater in historically red Texas. According to Civiqs, 57 percent of Texas voters disapprove of Trump’s job performance, while 36 percent approve, giving him a net rating of minus 21. Texas is set to benefit from a $22.3 billion combined-cycle gas-fired power plant backed by South Korea, which Trump announced last week along with other energy investments. The Project Star facility, to be located in Encinal, Texas, is intended to supply power directly to AI data centers. Trump won Texas by more than 13 points in 2024, but his approval ratings have been underwater in the state since May of last year, per Civiqs polling. Texas is also home to one of this year's closely watched Senate races, with Republican nominee Ken Paxton facing Democratic state Representative James Talarico. Ohio While unveiling details of the South Korean energy investments alongside Trump, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick named Ohio as one of the states set to benefit. Lutnick said that a combined $120 billion investment would go towards building eight “gigantic nuclear power plants” across the country, naming Ohio, Tennessee, South Carolina and Kentucky as potential locations. In Ohio, 55 percent of voters disapprove of Trump’s job performance, compared with 38 percent who approve. He has a net approval rating of minus 18. Trump won Ohio by about 11 points in 2024. The state is currently home to one of the most closely watched Senate races of the 2026 midterms, with Republican Senator Jon Husted facing former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown. Tennessee Tennessee is one of the states where Trump's approval rating comes closest to breaking even among those set to receive investment. Civiqs shows 47 percent of Tennessee voters disapproving of Trump, compared with 45 percent approving, leaving him with a net approval rating of minus 2 percentage points. Trump’s net approval rating remained positive in Tennessee until late August, per Civiqs. South Carolina Trump is also underwater in South Carolina, although by a narrower margin than in many of the other states set to receive investment. Civiqs shows 51 percent of South Carolina voters disapprove of Trump's job performance, while 42 percent approve, a net approval rating of minus 9 percentage points. Trump carried South Carolina by more than 17 points in 2024. Kentucky Kentucky was also among the states named by Lutnick as a potential location for the planned nuclear projects under the South Korea investment package. Civiqs found that 51 percent of Kentucky voters disapprove of Trump’s job performance, compared with 39 percent who approve, giving him a net approval rating of minus 12. Trump won Kentucky by more than 30 points in 2024. What's Next With early voting already underway or set to begin soon in several states, upcoming polling will more clearly indicate whether these investment commitments are shifting voter sentiment or whether Trump's approval ratings remain a headwind for Republican candidates heading into Election Day. news.title: Karoline Leavitt Goes to Fox—Full List of Trump Officials Linked to Network
news.text: Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt is joining Fox News, becoming the latest Trump administration official to join the conservative network. Leavitt, 29, who stepped down from her role as President Trump's chief spokesperson in August, will work as a contributor while providing commentary and analysis on Fox News Channel starting on November 1, the network announced Monday. "Karoline’s firsthand experience in the White House and on the presidential campaign trail gives her a distinct understanding of today’s political landscape," Fox News Media CEO Suzanne Scott told Newsweek in a statement. "We look forward to her providing our audience with authentic and sharp insight across all FOX News Media platforms." Leavitt, the youngest White House press secretary in history, becomes the most recent former Trump mouthpiece to work at Fox News, following in the footsteps of Kayleigh McEnany, who currently appears on "Outnumbered" and hosts "Saturday in America" on the network. On the other side of the political aisle, some former administration officials for President Joe Biden have also moved into roles at left-leaning networks, including White House press secretary Jen Psaki, who now hosts The Briefing with Jen Psaki on MS NOW, and Kete Bedingfield, Biden’s onetime communications director who later joined CNN as a political commentator. Jamal Simmons, who once served as Biden’s deputy assistant and Vice President Kamala Harris’ communications director, also works at CNN as a political contributor. Trump Officials Working With the Media Here's a closer look at notable Trump officials who later joined Fox or former network personalities now working in the president's second administration: Kayleigh McEnany McEnany, 38, served as press secretary from April 2020 through the end of Trump's first term and joined Fox News in 2021. While at the network, she's interviewed national figures like FBI Director Kash Patel, Vice President JD Vance and Second Lady Usha Vance, among others. More recently, McEnany also had an exclusive interview with Edward Paltzik, an attorney for Lindsay Clancy trial juror Michael Desronvil. Her program, Saturday in America, regularly competes as the top weekend cable news program among total viewers, according to the network. Larry Kudlow Kudlow, who previously served as assistant to the president for economic policy and director of the National Economic Council under President Trump, joined FOX Business Network in early 2021. He currently hosts Kudlow, where he dissects financial trends and the "impact facing households and businesses across the country," according to his network biography. Among other guests, Kudlow has hosted President Trump, billionaire Elon Musk, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and former Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin. Lara Trump The 43-year-old wife of Eric Trump and former co-chair of the Republican National Committee currently hosts My View with Lara Trump on Fox News, where she works as a "dedicated advocate for her family, animals and conservative values," according to her official network biography. She previously worked as a paid contributor, but left Fox when Donald Trump launched his 2024 presidential campaign and then returned in early 2025. Jeanine Pirro Pirro, who previously hosted Justice with Judge Jeanine on Fox, was appointed as interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia in May 2025 and confirmed by the Senate two months later. Trump elevated his longtime ally to D.C.'s top role last year after Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican, said he would not support interim attorney Ed Martin for a permanent position. Pirro marked the 23rd current or former Fox News employee Trump had recruited for his administration since taking office in January 2025, Newsweek reported last year. Pete Hegseth Hegseth, a former Fox News host and contributor, became the 29th secretary of defense in U.S. history in January 2025 after Vice President JD Vance broke a 50-50 vote in the Senate. He previously served as an infantry officer in the U.S. Army National Guard and had deployments in Guantanamo Bay, Iraq and Afghanistan, according to his official Pentagon biography, which does not include his tenure at the conservative network. Dan Bongino Bongino, a former police officer who previously hosted Unfiltered with Dan Bongino, left the network in 2023 to focus on his podcast. He later joined the FBI as deputy director in March 2025 before leaving the agency earlier this year. Sean Duffy Duffy, who has worked as secretary of transportation since January 2025, previously co-hosted The Bottom Line on Fox Business Channel before Trump tapped him to join the administration. His wife, Rachel Campos-Duffy, continues to appear as a host on Fox & Friends Weekend. Michael Waltz Waltz, who has served as the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations since September 2025, briefly worked as a paid Fox contributor the year before winning election to the House of Representatives in 2018. Tom Homan Tom Homan, the White House's current "border czar," had worked at Fox as a frequent contributor prior to being designated to his current role by Trump in November 2024. Others The Fox News-Trump pipeline has also included Michael Bastasch, a former writer at the network who later served as the senior adviser for communications at the Environmental Protection Agency, as well as Tammy Bruce, a State Department spokesperson who regularly appeared on Fox News, and Kimberly Guilfoyle, a staple of The Five who now serves as the U.S. ambassador to Greece. Keith Kellogg, a retired three-star general and frequent Fox News contributor, also served as the special envoy for Ukraine and Russia prior to leaving the administration in late 2025. What's Next Her hiring comes as Trump seeks to advance his second-term agenda ahead of crucial midterm contests that will determine control of Congress. Fox News has not announced how frequently Leavitt will appear on air or whether her contributor role could eventually expand into a larger hosting position, as it has for some former administration officials who joined the network. news.title: Experts tracked $80M of spending on almost 170 AI‑generated midterm ads. It got weird
news.text:
The 2026 U.S. midterm campaigns are the first in which AI-generated political ads are regularly appearing on people’s televisions and social media feeds.

We are researchers who have been studying political advertising through the Wesleyan Media Project since 2010. This election cycle – using data from media reports, student coders and AdImpact, a firm that tracks political ad spending – we’ve tracked about $80 million in spending on almost 170 unique ads that use AI.

What we found has surprised us: AI use spans from hyperrealistic deepfakes to subtle enhancements; Republican sponsors – both candidates and interest groups – are much more likely to use AI than are Democratic sponsors; and, thanks to a patchwork of state legislation, many of these ads do not disclose the use of AI at all.

An assortment of politicians and watchdog groups have expressed concern about campaigns using generative AI to produce deepfakes – synthetic videos showing people doing things they did not do – that might deceive voters.

We’ve noticed several ads containing hyperrealistic deepfakes of famous politicians, including Donald Trump, Nancy Pelosi, Barack Obama, Kamala Harris and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Ocasio-Cortez, in particular, is a favorite among Republican advertisers, appearing in at least five ads.

We’ve seen deepfakes in which a Republican Senate candidate from Louisiana drives a school bus full of undocumented immigrants, a Republican candidate for governor from South Carolina walks arm in arm with drag queens, and an ad in which Liz Cheney, Mitt Romney and Mike Pence are seen carrying pitchforks on the White House lawn.

People who are not politicians made appearances, too, including a fake Dr. Anthony Fauci, seen running around a state fair with a huge syringe, presumably eager to vaccinate everyone. We’ve also noticed several ads in which AI was used to generate crowds or constituents.

In several cases, AI was used to enhance visuals rather than generate something new. One ad from Chip Keating, a Republican candidate for governor in Oklahoma, includes an AI disclaimer, but it doesn’t specify exactly how AI was used. Ads that use AI to enhance visuals don’t necessarily look different from ads that were created in the pre-AI era, which makes it difficult for viewers to discern whether they depict something false.

Republicans – both candidates and groups such as super PACs and 501(c) organizations – are much more likely to use AI in their ads than are Democrats, according to our research.

In fact, Republican candidates or pro-Republican groups were behind 80% of the ads we tracked and 83% of the spending.

We can only speculate as to why Republicans dominate the use of AI in political advertising in 2026. In general, Democrats tend to take on a regulatory mindset when it comes to political campaigns, favoring limits on campaign spending and required disclosures. In 2022, for instance, only Senate Democrats and two independents voted to advance the DISCLOSE Act that would have required additional campaign finance disclosures for super PACs, labor unions and corporations. Republicans, by contrast, tend to be more in favor of a free market approach.

These more general philosophies may be reflected in the parties’ use of generative AI for political advertising, something about which voters are worried. Polling shows broad support for more regulation, with 78% of registered voters favoring a ban on AI content that makes deceptive claims about candidates.

Because regulation of AI in advertising depends on a patchwork of state legislation, many of these ads are not required to disclose the use of AI. This lack of disclaimers makes tracking AI use in ads challenging. Our team has relied on media coverage and trained student coders to flag ads that are potentially AI-generated.

Across 35 states, only 31% of the ads we tracked – representing 22% of the spending – disclosed the use of AI tools. The wording of these disclaimers was all over the map. For example, one Georgia ad included the disclaimer, “This video has been manipulated or generated with artificial intelligence,” while an Oklahoma ad said, “Political satire. AI-generated images do not depict actual events.” A North Carolina state Senate ad said, “You guessed it! AI was definitely used to generate these silly video clips.”

Some advertisers voluntarily disclose the use of AI even when they are not required to do so. Sometimes, the opposite occurs – advertisers don’t include disclaimers even when state law requires them to. In fact, we’ve found that a state law that requires disclaimers on ads that use AI has very little relationship with the actual use of disclaimers.

In states without laws governing the use of AI in political ads, 32% of ads contained a disclaimer; by contrast, in states with laws governing the use of AI, 29% contained a disclaimer. This comparison, however, is not perfect, as some of the ads in our database aren’t covered by their state’s law. Some states, such as Colorado, have laws that apply only to candidate deepfakes and thus exclude other uses of AI. In other instances, such as in Louisiana, an AI law was enacted after the ad aired.

Minnesota law generally bans deepfakes in political ads, but an ad featuring synthetic video of Democratic Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan aired in May 2026 anyway. Whether it violated state law is uncertain, as the law requires that the media be “so realistic that a reasonable person would believe it depicts speech or conduct of an individual who did not in fact engage in such speech or conduct.”

Moving forward, the real policy challenge will revolve around transparency, the enforceability of existing laws and simply figuring out what type of disclosure would be helpful to voters.
news.summary: Republican candidates or pro-Republican groups were behind 80% of the ads we tracked and 83% of the spending
