news.title: Woke Maryland activist blasted for shocking race gaffe that saw her rail against 'white man' who is actually black
news.text:
A Maryland-based activist has been slammed online after she railed against a black man whom she assumed was white. 

Tiffany Carlock, who goes by Candidly Tiff online, shared a video of Rage Against the Machine guitarist Tom Morello telling Rolling Stone that he 'certainly did not' vote for Kamala Harris in the 2024 election. 

'I certainly did not... I couldn't do it. V for vendetta. That one inch, that one inch of who you are belongs to you, and they can't have it,' Morello, a left-wing political activist, stated. 

Carlock then posted the clip to her X account and wrote: 'I don't know who this white man is, but I'm not surprised he didn't vote for Kamala in the 2024 election. Like many others, he chose to say f*** you to the rest of us.' 

Online users quickly flocked to the comments, letting Carlock know that Morello is black. 

His late mother, Mary Morello, was of Italian and Irish descent, and his father, Ngethe Njoroge, served as Kenya's first ambassador to the United Nations.

'He is exactly as black as Kamala Harris,' someone posted. 

'Tom Morello is Black. Guitarist for RATM and Audioslave. Harvard educated,' another wrote. 

'That is a black man,' a commenter said. 

Another person shared: 'He's mixed race. He's been fighting for justice his entire life.' 

'He's the guitarist for Rage Against the Machine. His dad is Kenyon [sic]. This is his politics. He's always been like this,' a user wrote. 

But Carlock seemed to brush off the criticism she received after saying that she was aware that Morello is biracial.

'He is *half* white and *half* black, my bad...doesn't change anything still don't know this man and he said f*** the rest of us. That makes it even more disappointing.' 

She went on to reply to one of the commenters, stating: 'Interesting he looks white and sounds ignorant.' 

Before his confession, the rocker, 62, described why he couldn't stand behind Harris and the Democratic Party. 

'I saw how the corporate Democrat sausage is made. It is worse than you think. And there is a reason - there is a righteous fury at the corporate-controlled, money-controlled electoral system we have that is absolutely illegitimate, and people cannot choke down voting for a candidate - I understand it - that is responsible for what happened in Gaza,' he stated. 

'Now, I live in a state where it may not have moved the meter, but I just couldn't do it. Couldn't do it,' he said, referring to his home state of California. 

When asked when he last voted for a Democratic candidate, Morello said: 'I don't, can't remember the last time I did.' 

The Rolling Stone journalist quipped that Morello's voting decision might be 'a point of disagreement with Bruce Springsteen' - another famous rock star who endorsed Harris in the recent election. 

'No, I mean yeah, but that's not - I think he's doing the right thing, how his political and personal barometer leads him, and so am I. 

'And I respect that. And I think he respects my point of view,' the guitarist said of Springsteen. 

Morello's comments came around the same time as the debut of his Power to People festival that was hosted in Maryland on Saturday. 

He and other iconic rockers, including Springsteen, the Foo Fighters, and Soundgarden, came out to support the celebration of peace and justice that is aimed at promoting voter turnout ahead of November's midterm elections. 

Carlock is no stranger to sharing her political views online and has been referred to as 'a Maryland-based grassroots political advocate and unapologetic truth-teller,' according to MD Dems. 

She also hosts a weekly segment on her YouTube page called 'Fired Up Friday,' where she discusses current events and politics. 

The Daily Mail contacted Carlock and Morello for comment.
news.summary: Tiffany Carlock, a political activist from Maryland who goes by Candidly Tiff online, was blasted by users after she railed against a black man that she assumed was white.

WASHINGTON—During an address to the nation Tuesday in which he claimed to have obtained definitive proof that the election was stolen, President Donald Trump presented bombshell evidence showing his opponent Joe Biden actively campaigned against him throughout the 2020 presidential race.

Trump, who spoke from the White House, detailed a conspiracy in which paid operatives and officials from every level of government—including at least three former U.S. presidents—participated in a highly coordinated effort to convince Americans to cast their votes for Biden. Trump alleged that members of this shadowy group regularly called and emailed voters to dissuade them from voting for him, part of a plot to ensure the Democratic nominee would be victorious at the polls on Election Day.

“This is a huge scheme, maybe the biggest, most illegal scheme anybody has ever seen,” said Trump, who later posted images of campaign mailers, yard signs, and the 2020 Democratic National Convention on Truth Social to support his assertion that Biden worked to turn voters against him. “For months, Crooked Joe went all over the country saying very nasty things about me: that I wasn’t fit to be president, that I was failing on Covid. Joe was telling everybody he should be president, not me. Right out in the open. He wasn’t even hiding it.”

“He went after people with speeches, television, the internet, all of it, and this reduced my votes while increasing his votes,” the president added. “Very, very fraudulent.”

According to Trump, Biden realized early on that he could sway the results of the 2020 election if he got a majority of Americans to support him, and so he took advantage of this vulnerability in the system by seeking to influence voter opinion. The president contended that at Biden’s behest, hundreds of millions of dollars were funneled into anti-Trump propaganda, which included unflattering videos broadcast on public airwaves that suggested Trump did not have the skills or temperament necessary to hold office.

“They called them ‘attack ads,’” Trump said. “Attack. Very violent word.”

As he stood at a podium in the Roosevelt Room, a TV played a compilation of the 2020 ads, which the president described as “totally deceptive,” saying Biden’s co-conspirators had selectively used footage of Trump praising white supremacists as “fine people” or downplaying a pandemic killing 1,000 Americans a day and had completely ignored his first-term achievements. An aide periodically paused the footage so the president could circle his own face with a laser pointer.

“It’s cheating,” Trump said of an ad in which he could be seen mocking a disabled reporter. “They picked the things people liked least and showed them over and over. But they kept out the beautiful things, the many, many perfect things. They didn’t show me cutting the ribbon. They didn’t show me getting into a helicopter. That’s election interference.”

“People see a Biden commercial, hear a Biden speech, and suddenly millions of ballots appear with his name checked instead of mine,” he continued. “Without those ballots, I win every single state. It’s a blowout.”

Trump went on to accuse celebrities, donors, and groups such as Joe Biden for President 2020 of serving as accomplices, describing a “vast criminal enterprise” that maintained offices in all 50 states and employed thousands of people who systematically studied voter lists, operated phone banks, and knocked on the doors of prospective supporters. According to the president, Biden’s organized crime ring even included his wife, Jill, and his running mate, Kamala Harris, both of whom joined him in campaigning against Trump.

“There were very powerful people helping to do it, to rig it,” Trump said. “Barack Hussein Obama, I’ve seen video, he went onstage before thousands of voters and said, ‘Don’t vote for Donald Trump, let’s fight like hell not to have it.’ And Michelle did the same. So did LeBron. The deep state—a very, very famous group of people, in many cases—they were doing it. They endorse Biden, and then Biden wins? That’s no coincidence. That’s the greatest scam in this country’s history.”

Reached for comment, many of the president’s advisors defended his assessment, saying American elections were too susceptible to this kind of fraud.

“The electoral system is a disaster,” White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino told reporters. “One candidate spends a year saying terrible things about the other candidate, promises people things, asks for their votes, and if enough people vote for him, they let him become president. How is that secure? Thankfully, Donald Trump won’t rest until we have a system where nobody can unseat the person already in the Oval Office.”

news.title: Democrats Inch Into Red Territory, but Have Problems on Home Turf
news.text:
With a month to go before the midterm elections, the U.S. map keeps shifting in Democrats’ favor. Senate seats in states that President Trump won comfortably are now seen as tossups and House seats that he carried by double digits are in danger of flipping.

At the same time, Democrats are struggling to coalesce around an ideological platform and face a steep financial disadvantage to Republicans. In some blue-leaning states, Senate GOP candidates are staging strong challenges, giving Republicans hope of potentially tempering any Democratic gains elsewhere—and forcing Democrats to devote money and energy to defending their home turf.

“While many have long predicted that Democrats will enjoy a ‘blue wave’ election, I think of it more as a ‘red undertow,’ which will pull many Republicans under and significantly trim the margins for many others,” Charlie Cook, the founder of the nonpartisan Cook Political Report wrote recently. “A blue wave implies an endorsement or affirmation of Democrats and their policies. But Democrats’ brand is still in tatters.”

GOP held early Senate advantage

At the start of the year, the Senate map looked difficult for Democrats. Republicans have a 53-47 majority, while Democrats had few obvious pickup opportunities and were also playing defense in a number of states.

They had to defend Sen. Jon Ossoff in battleground Georgia and hold on to open seats in New Hampshire, Michigan and Minnesota. They saw the open North Carolina seat as a good target, and their best chance to take out a Republican was Sen. Susan Collins in Maine—but that was always going to be hard. Collins easily dispatched her Democratic opponent last time, and the Democratic leadership and grassroots were divided over the best candidate to take her on.

To get a majority, Democrats would have to make inroads in states that Trump had won, in most cases by wide margins. The Democratic Party was also struggling to excite its voters and donors, and there were signs that the party’s left flank was gaining ground—potentially turning off independents.

A blue shift after U.S. strikes Iran

Trump launched the war with Iran at the end of February. Gas prices surged, and voters questioned whether he was breaking his pledge to keep the U.S. out of “forever wars” overseas. Trump also struggled to bring down high costs, and mortgage rates on homes hit new highs. His own polling has plummeted, including in states where a majority of voters had supported him.

Republicans also struggled with candidate recruitment and divisive primaries. In Texas, Trump supported scandal-plagued Attorney General Ken Paxton over sitting Sen. John Cornyn in what became a nasty primary fight. Paxton ultimately won, making the race more competitive for the Democratic candidate.

All those developments put more red states in play. Democrats also grew increasingly confident about keeping Georgia in their column and picking up North Carolina, where former Gov. Roy Cooper looked strong. Alaska, Texas and Iowa were solidly on the radar as potential flips. Even some deep red states started to appear competitive, such as Kansas. Still, past polling showing Democratic strength in red states has proved illusory, tempering expectations.

“The map gets better every day,” Democratic strategist Caitlin Legacki said. But given polling misses in primaries and recent cycles, “I think it’s really, really dangerous for Democrats to start counting our chickens.”

Map grows but Democrats struggle to close the deal on home turf

At the same time, Democrats have had candidate issues of their own. Graham Platner, a progressive-leaning oyster farmer, bucked the party establishment to become the Democratic nominee in Maine until an allegation of sexual assault forced him out of the race. Maine voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024, but GOP Sen. Susan Collins remains formidable. She is facing Democrats’ new candidate, former state Senate President Troy Jackson, in what is rated a tossup.

In Michigan, a far-left candidate beat out the establishment choice to become the Democratic nominee. But the candidacy of Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official, has divided the Democratic Party, and analysts say Republicans have a shot at winning the seat. New Hampshire Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas was seen as the Democratic establishment’s choice, but he is locked in a tight race against Republican former Sen. John Sununu.

Analysts still give Democrats a slight edge in both Michigan and New Hampshire.

The current snapshot

Democrats’ inroads in red areas and Republicans’ continued hope in blue ones have left the Senate up for grabs.

If Democrats gain control of the Senate, they would have significant power to block or reshape Trump’s agenda, control the chamber’s committees and influence judicial and executive-branch appointments. They also could use their investigative and oversight powers to scrutinize the administration’s conduct.

The House has long looked like a more likely pickup for Democrats, even as the GOP is expected to make gains from redistricting. Democrats only need a handful of seats to flip the majority, and historically the party that controls the White House—in this case, Republicans—almost always loses members in the midterm elections.

That House map has continued to expand entering the fall, with Democrats now playing in districts that Trump won by double digits just two years ago. The Cook Political Report projects Democrats will flip a net of five to 15 seats, giving them 220 to 230 in the next Congress.

Working against Democrats is their financial gap with Republicans, with GOP committees and super PACs far outraising their Democratic counterparts. GOP groups, including the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc., have unleashed their cash this fall, pouring money into tight House and Senate races in the hopes of turning the tide in their favor.

Money can change the race, “but it doesn’t always,” said Doug Heye, a former communications director for the Republican National Committee. “You’re trying to fortify a levy to prevent water from coming over, and it’s a hard thing to do,” Heye said.

news.title: We’ve tracked $80M of spending on almost 170 AI-generated political ads this year – it’s weird
news.text:
The 2026 U.S. midterm campaigns are the first in which AI-generated political ads are regularly appearing on people’s televisions and social media feeds.

We are researchers who have been studying political advertising through the Wesleyan Media Project since 2010. This election cycle – using data from media reports, student coders and AdImpact, a firm that tracks political ad spending – we’ve tracked about US$80 million in spending on almost 170 unique ads that use AI. 

What we found has surprised us: AI use spans from hyperrealistic deepfakes to subtle enhancements; Republican sponsors – both candidates and interest groups – are much more likely to use AI than are Democratic sponsors; and, thanks to a patchwork of state legislation, many of these ads do not disclose the use of AI at all.

From deepfakes to subtle edits

An assortment of politicians and watchdog groups have expressed concern about campaigns using generative AI to produce deepfakes – synthetic videos showing people doing things they did not do – that might deceive voters.

We’ve noticed several ads containing hyperrealistic deepfakes of famous politicians, including Donald Trump, Nancy Pelosi, Barack Obama, Kamala Harris and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Ocasio-Cortez, in particular, is a favorite among Republican advertisers, appearing in at least five ads.

We’ve seen deepfakes in which a Republican Senate candidate from Louisiana drives a school bus full of undocumented immigrants, a Republican candidate for governor from South Carolina walks arm in arm with drag queens, and an ad in which Liz Cheney, Mitt Romney and Mike Pence are seen carrying pitchforks on the White House lawn. 

People who are not politicians made appearances, too, including a fake Dr. Anthony Fauci, seen running around a state fair with a huge syringe, presumably eager to vaccinate everyone. We’ve also noticed several ads in which AI was used to generate crowds or constituents.

In several cases, AI was used to enhance visuals rather than generate something new. One ad from Chip Keating, a Republican candidate for governor in Oklahoma, includes an AI disclaimer, but it doesn’t specify exactly how AI was used. Ads that use AI to enhance visuals don’t necessarily look different from ads that were created in the pre-AI era, which makes it difficult for viewers to discern whether they depict something false. 

A partisan gap

Republicans – both candidates and groups such as super PACs and 501(c) organizations – are much more likely to use AI in their ads than are Democrats, according to our research. 

In fact, Republican candidates or pro-Republican groups were behind 80% of the ads we tracked and 83% of the spending. 

We can only speculate as to why Republicans dominate the use of AI in political advertising in 2026. In general, Democrats tend to take on a regulatory mindset when it comes to political campaigns, favoring limits on campaign spending and required disclosures. In 2022, for instance, only Senate Democrats and two independents voted to advance the DISCLOSE Act that would have required additional campaign finance disclosures for super PACs, labor unions and corporations. Republicans, by contrast, tend to be more in favor of a free market approach.

These more general philosophies may be reflected in the parties’ use of generative AI for political advertising, something about which voters are worried. Polling shows broad support for more regulation, with 78% of registered voters favoring a ban on AI content that makes deceptive claims about candidates. 

Disclaimers all over the map

Because regulation of AI in advertising depends on a patchwork of state legislation, many of these ads are not required to disclose the use of AI. This lack of disclaimers makes tracking AI use in ads challenging. Our team has relied on media coverage and trained student coders to flag ads that are potentially AI-generated.

Across 35 states, only 31% of the ads we tracked – representing 22% of the spending – disclosed the use of AI tools. The wording of these disclaimers was all over the map. For example, one Georgia ad included the disclaimer, “This video has been manipulated or generated with artificial intelligence,” while an Oklahoma ad said, “Political satire. AI-generated images do not depict actual events.” A North Carolina state Senate ad said, “You guessed it! AI was definitely used to generate these silly video clips.” 

Laws don’t drive disclosure

Some advertisers voluntarily disclose the use of AI even when they are not required to do so. Sometimes, the opposite occurs – advertisers don’t include disclaimers even when state law requires them to. In fact, we’ve found that a state law that requires disclaimers on ads that use AI has very little relationship with the actual use of disclaimers.

In states without laws governing the use of AI in political ads, 32% of ads contained a disclaimer; by contrast, in states with laws governing the use of AI, 29% contained a disclaimer. This comparison, however, is not perfect, as some of the ads in our database aren’t covered by their state’s law. Some states, such as Colorado, have laws that apply only to candidate deepfakes and thus exclude other uses of AI. In other instances, such as in Louisiana, an AI law was enacted after the ad aired.

Minnesota law generally bans deepfakes in political ads, but an ad featuring synthetic video of Democratic Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan aired in May 2026 anyway. Whether it violated state law is uncertain, as the law requires that the media be “so realistic that a reasonable person would believe it depicts speech or conduct of an individual who did not in fact engage in such speech or conduct.”

Moving forward, the real policy challenge will revolve around transparency, the enforceability of existing laws and simply figuring out what type of disclosure would be helpful to voters.
news.summary: Almost 170 ads and $80 million in spending and only 31% with a disclaimer: Here’s what researchers found when they tracked AI in this year’s campaign ads.

news.title: ‘I’m here to save lives’: Inside the unlikely Biden-Trump partnership to secure a Gaza ceasefire
news.text:
Secure rooms in the US Capitol are cavernous compared to the White House Situation Room. They are designed for full committees or larger gatherings, not intimate discussions. On Nov. 20, 2024, Jake Sullivan and I had gone to one of those rooms to brief our successors two weeks after Donald Trump resoundingly defeated Kamala Harris.

Sullivan was Biden’s national security advisor. His named successor was Mike Waltz, a congressman from Florida. I was Biden’s lead on the Middle East and a chief negotiator on talks to free hostages held by Hamas in Gaza in exchange for a ceasefire with Israel. My named successor was Steve Witkoff — a real-estate tycoon and Trump’s best friend.

Shortly after the election, I had called Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and former Middle East hand. My message was that we had a chance to secure a Gaza deal so long as we could be seen as working together without any daylight between the incoming and outgoing teams. That was a tall order given the polarization in Washington, but it was the only chance we had — and for the first time in months, circumstances trended in our favor.

The hostage talks had collapsed in August, when shortly after Biden, together with the leaders of Egypt and Qatar, presented a new proposal endorsed by Israel, Hamas terrorists murdered six hostages in a tunnel under Rafah, a city in southern Gaza. One of those hostages was Hersh Goldberg-Polin, an American who had been grievously wounded and lost an arm in Hamas’s attacks at the Nova music festival on Oct. 7, 2023, before being taken captive.

Following the collapse of the negotiations, Israel had won a string of military victories. It started on Sept. 17, 2024, with an operation that exploded thousands of beepers carried by Hezbollah militants in Lebanon. I first heard about what became known as Operation Grim Beeper from a contact in Mossad, Israel’s external intelligence service, who told me, “We just blew the dicks off Hezbollah.”

In many cases, that was not metaphorical.

Hezbollah, like Hamas, a terrorist group backed by Iran, had made the fateful decision to join in the Hamas attack on Israel. On Oct. 8, 2023, it began firing daily rocket barrages into northern Israel, eventually displacing nearly 80,000 people. Israel had been prepared to forgo an operation against Hezbollah if there was a hostage deal. But with no deal in sight, Israel soon followed the beeper operation with a ground assault into the Hezbollah strongholds of southern Lebanon.

By the end of September, Hezbollah’s leader, Hassan Nasrallah, was dead, together with most of his senior lieutenants, buried in an underground Beirut compound.

On Oct. 1, following Nasrallah’s death, Iran made its own foolish — and fateful — decision to launch another massive ballistic missile attack against Israel, following on a failed attack it had launched months earlier. This time, Iran launched nearly two hundred missiles at once, exceeding its earlier salvo.

In the Situation Room that afternoon, as interceptors destroyed incoming missiles at the edge of outer space, we received reports of a direct hit on a college dormitory in Tel Aviv. I was seated just across from Harris, less than five weeks from Election Day. She mouthed, “Oh, shit.” We knew that if Iran inflicted significant Israeli casualties, the Israelis were prepared to launch a massive counterattack into Iran.

Fortunately, that report, like many first reports, was wrong. Only remnants of a destroyed missile struck the building, causing little damage. The attack was mostly defeated, dismaying the Iranians, who had believed their larger salvo of missiles would be successful.

About two weeks later, on Oct. 16, Israeli forces killed Hamas’s leader, Yahya Sinwar. He was found in Rafah, not far from where Hersh and five other hostages had been shot to death in a tunnel. Sinwar’s death removed a major obstacle to a deal — him — and allowed the Israelis to be more flexible on some terms now that the mastermind of the Oct. 7 attacks could no longer reclaim power. For Israel, it was akin to the United States military killing Osama bin Laden after 9/11.

Finally, on Oct. 26, Israel conducted stealth air attacks against Iran, targeting and destroying many of its strategic air defense systems. We worked closely with the Israelis on this counterattack, walking the Israelis back from a more aggressive response.

Biden told Netanyahu that we would deploy more air defenses to Israel and received assurance from Netanyahu in return that Israel’s response would focus on Iran’s own air defense batteries. The aim was to change the balance of power without triggering a wider war. We messaged Iran’s leaders afterward that their country was now wide open to air attacks should Israel (or the United States) choose to launch them. With Russia bogged down in Ukraine, Iran could not soon replace the destroyed air defense batteries, most of which were Russian and had proved ineffective against Israel’s capabilities. Iran never responded to Israel’s counterattack.

With the tables turned on Iran, Sinwar dead, and Hezbollah’s leadership decimated, we predicted that Hezbollah would soon accept a ceasefire deal with Israel. That would be the moment to return to the Gaza deal — picking up where we had left off in August.

My case to Kushner was straightforward. If Israel and Hamas knew that Trump would implement the deal on the table, we had a chance to close it before he took office. But if not, we would lose the best chance we had had since the war began. It was time to seize the moment, and the only way to do that was by working together.

Kushner fully agreed.

He told me that he would not be joining the new administration but said my successor on the Middle East was someone close to Trump, a pragmatic problem-solver who would want to work with me to the extent appropriate. He did not mention Witkoff, whose name emerged days later as Trump’s likely Middle East envoy.

Biden invited Trump to the Oval on Nov. 13, 2024, mostly for a one-on-one. When the cameras came in briefly, Biden promised a smooth transition. “Politics is tough,” Trump said. “And it’s in many cases not a very nice world, but it is a nice world today, and I appreciate very much a transition that is so smooth, it’ll be as smooth as it can get.”

I saw Biden afterward. Unlike many Democrats at the time who saw the election as an existential disaster, Biden — at least with me — was focused on working with the incoming team wherever we could. That was especially so on the hostage crisis.

According to Biden, the two presidents agreed to coordinate, setting the stage for my meeting with Sullivan, Waltz, and Witkoff seven days later.

In the secure room at the Capitol, Sullivan snapped open a document pouch and arrayed briefing materials in front of him, including maps of the region and background on Iran’s nuclear program. We sat alone at a large table, waiting for Trump’s team to arrive.

Waltz entered, followed by Witkoff. The former was a retired military officer with perfect hair and rod-straight posture. The latter was a brash real estate developer known for carrying a pistol in a sock through the alleys and streets of New York, where he built a multibillion-dollar empire. Both exhibited a lighthearted manner, something that I had lost handling the Gaza crisis, where tens of thousands had died, over one hundred hostages remained in tunnels underground and the region stood on the brink of an all-out war.

The meeting began awkwardly, the four of us standing at the corner of the large table in the oversize room, introducing ourselves by titles. Waltz took his seat, and we followed.

“Trump told us to solve everything, that’s our mission,” Witkoff said, laughing.

“Solve it!” Waltz added.

Senator JD Vance, the incoming vice president, popped in unexpectedly. We stood. He asked what we were talking about, and when we said the Middle East, he told us that was his cue to leave. (Run as fast as you can, I thought.) Vance, Waltz, and Witkoff discussed recent calls they’d each had with Trump, comparing notes on what they had heard — apparently different things. The calls had come at all hours, and Waltz asked both men whether Trump ever slept. Witkoff answered, “I’ve known him for forty years, the answer is — no, not very much.”

“Force of nature,” Waltz remarked.

Witkoff explained that he had been Trump’s real-estate attorney before branching out on his own. “I’ve had success, but there’s only one Trump,” he told us. Vance came around the table to shake my hand, and Sullivan’s. He said he wanted to work with us during the transition period, which seemed sincere, and then left the room.

With a map on the table, Sullivan walked through what had changed in the Middle East since the hostage talks collapsed in August. It was head-spinning even for those of us who had been living and breathing the issues every day since then. For Witkoff, I recounted my difficult experience on the hostage talks, and explained why we might now, finally, have a shot.

Of course, for that to happen we had to be seen — by both Hamas and Israel — as working together, as both parties would demand to know Trump’s views.

“The only reason I’m here is to save lives,” Witkoff said. “It’s the most noble thing anyone can do with their life, to save another life. So, I’m all in, count on it.”

He asked what we needed from him, and from Trump. I took out the text. Every detail of a carefully negotiated agreement — from the extent of Israel’s redeployment during a ceasefire, to the timing and sequence of hostages and prisoner exchanges, to the minute-by-minute details on delivery of humanitarian assistance with the guns silent — was reflected in a package of texts that had been hammered over months shuttling between Doha, Jerusalem, and Cairo.

The outstanding issue was agreement from Hamas on the hostages to come out during the first stage of the ceasefire, a category that included women, the elderly, and the sick or wounded, something the group still had never seriously engaged on. There would not be a hostage deal, I explained, without an agreed list of the hostages to be released.

Witkoff claimed that he knew most of the leaders in the Middle East from his real-estate business, and he asked whether we’d be comfortable with his traveling to the region to reengage and to preview his new role. Sullivan said that would be fine, so long as he was not negotiating, and kept in close contact with me before and afterward. Witkoff wrote down his number, and we agreed to speak regularly from that moment forward.

For the remainder of the briefing, we discussed Iran. With Trump entering office and Iran now vulnerable to direct attack, the Israelis believed Tehran might race to enrich uranium to weapons grade — the precursor for a nuclear bomb. Throughout the crisis, since Oct. 7, Iran had been enriching uranium to 60% grade, a step away from the 90% required for a bomb. It was the only country in the world without a weapons program to do so.

The previous week, Sullivan had convened the Principals Committee to war-game the scenario of Iran enriching to weapons grade. Participants were unanimous that if we saw such indications, we’d recommend a US military strike against Iran’s nuclear facilities, including its deeply buried facility at Fordow. The operation had been rehearsed over the past year should the president — or a future president — need it. We dispatched a message to Iran’s leaders warning them not to think about escalating their nuclear program.

Witkoff raised his hands. “Trump says I’ve got Iran, but maybe I don’t want it. Are you f**king kidding with all of this?”

Finally, Saudi Arabia. We reviewed a package of agreements that we had completed on a deal for normalization between Israel and Saudi Arabia, before the Oct. 7 crisis. I explained that the deal might be possible over Trump’s term, so long as Gaza could be settled. Netanyahu’s hard-right coalition government made everything more difficult, but it might not outlast Israel’s next election in 2026. (These elections are now scheduled for later this month.)

Witkoff came around to my side of the table. He extended his hand: “I’m here to save lives. I don’t give one shit about politics. If we save one life, we save the world.”

The table was now set for that, I assured him.

news.title: Navarro: The Jobs Report Reveals Federal Reserve Election Interference
news.text:
Authored by Peter Navarro via RealClearMarkets,

CNBC and Yahoo Finance called the jobs report a miss. Fox said it was lower than expected. More bad analysis from a Keynesian financial press that has shown extraordinary supply-side ignorance throughout the Trump 47 term.

The deeper story is indeed more complicated - and considerably more reassuring.

Start with the unemployment rate. It rose a tenth not because people lost jobs but because people came looking for them. The labor force participation rate jumped two tenths to 61.8 percent, well above expectations.

Behind the curtain, the share of prime-age Americans holding a job rose three tenths to 80.7 percent; for prime-age men, four tenths to 86.2 percent. When more people enter the labor force than the economy can hire in a single month, the unemployment rate rises. That is not weakness. That is Americans coming off the sidelines.

Now the headline number itself. Wall Street still reads payrolls through a Biden-era lens, when open borders swelled the labor force and the economy had to create well over 100,000 jobs a month just to stand still.

That world is gone. With the border secured and the population aging, the breakeven pace of job creation - the number that holds unemployment steady - has fallen to roughly 40,000 a month by most estimates, and the Dallas Fed puts it near zero. This month's 29,000 is well within the neighborhood of breakeven.

Now consider the composition: private employers added 46,000 jobs in September while government shed 17,000. Under Biden Wokenomics, government hiring padded the headline month after month. Under Trumpnomics, the private sector carries the load and the public payroll shrinks. That is exactly the right direction.

Then there is the industrial turn, which the headline - and the anti-Trump media - hides every month and which matters most. Manufacturing added 9,000 jobs in September, bringing this year's gain to roughly 72,000, after the sector lost more than 200,000 jobs in the last two years of the Biden administration.

Ahead of those production jobs comes the construction that makes them possible. Nonresidential specialty trade contractors, the electricians, pipefitters and concrete crews who build factories, added 12,300 jobs in September and are up nearly 112,000 since January 2025.

The factory-construction numbers of 2025 and 2026 are the manufacturing payrolls of 2027 and 2028. Real fixed private investment, up 2.3 percent in 2024 and 3.8 percent in 2025, is running at a 6.9 percent annual rate this year.

And a MAGA White House - built on blue-collar America - loves this: the unemployment rate for Americans without a high school diploma has fallen two and a half points over the year to 4.3 percent, the lowest on record.

Moreover, initial jobless claims, measured against the size of the workforce, are the lowest since the data began in 1967. Employers are holding on to the workers they have.

Nominal weekly earnings for manufacturing workers are up 5 percent, too, over the year, nearly 6 percent for production and nonsupervisory workers, while construction workers' earnings are up 4.7 percent.

Against the latest CPI - 3.4 percent headline, 2.4 percent core - those gains are comfortably positive in real terms, roughly 1 to 2½ percent after inflation. Solid, and no sign of a wage-price spiral.

Yet the newly minted Warsh Fed hiked rates in September into the teeth of an oil shock, breaking the Greenspan-Bernanke-Navarro rule: watch the second-round effects of an energy spike before you attack the first round.

This jobs report is the second-round evidence. There is no demand-side inflation for a rate hike to cure, and NOTHING in Friday's report offers a reason to tighten again in October.

Which raises the question: who is really running the Fed? The Trump-appointed chairman, who certainly must know better than to hike rates now? Or is Warsh leading from behind, appeasing a group of partisan anti-Trump Fed governors?

Remember that on September 18, 2024 - 48 days before Election Day - the Fed cut the federal-funds target by 50 basis points, from 5.25-5.50 percent to 4.75-5.00 percent. It was the first rate cut since March 2020. It was larger than the quarter-point move most forecasters expected, and it was a blatant attempt to help a hapless Kamala Harris beat Donald John Trump.

Now the Fed is interfering again, this time in the midterm elections. The September 16 hike has come again 48 days before Election Day - the same 48 days as in 2024. How other than politics do you explain a Fed rate hike on the eve of an election unsupported by the data and in flagrant violation of the Greenspan-Bernanke-Navarro rule?

There, I said it. And it damn well needs to be said.

news.title: You might need a weatherman to know how this Minnesota Senate district blows
news.text:
Austin Peterson’s mild verbal miscue revealed the challenge the Republican candidate faces in unseating DFLer Rob Kupec for a seat in the Minnesota Senate representing Moorhead in this election.

During a League of Women Voters candidate forum at the Moorhead Public Library last month, an audience member asked, “How will you stand up to President Trump and the federal government when they trample on Minnesotan’s rights?”

“Regardless of who the president is two years from now it will not be President Trump,” Peterson replied. “And so looking forward to that – well, looking beyond that, excuse me.”

But by the time Peterson uttered “looking forward,” a swath of voters in the packed meeting room laughed and then cheered the pending departure of a president with a 38% approval rating in Minnesota, according to a KSTP/Survey USA poll. 

“Some of you are probably looking forward to that,” Peterson acknowledged, which drew further hoots and hollers.

Kupec and Peterson are seeking to represent District 4, which represents the growing city of Moorhead, plus smaller cities and townships including Audubon, Comstock, Detroit Lakes, Dilworth, Glyndon, and Hawley.

Related: Why it will be hard, in a midterm likely to herald change, to oust a congressional incumbent in Minnesota

Moorhead is the county seat of Clay County, one of only nine counties in the entire U.S. to vote for the winning presidential candidate in every election between 2000 and 2020. The streak was broken in 2024 when Clay narrowly went for Kamala Harris and Tim Walz.

The DFL Senate Caucus and the Minnesota Senate Republican Committee each identified District 4 as one of a handful of toss-up races that will determine control of the Senate over the next four years. 

Kupec was elected in his first run for any political office in 2022, garnering 52% of the vote to Republican Dan Bohmer’s 47%. 

Kupec, a meteorologist, said he had the wind at his back in 2022 following the Supreme Court decision to let states set their own abortion laws. 

“I’m knocking on doors in Detroit Lakes, and I’m having a lot of angry women answering the doors, even in the more conservative side of the district,” Kupec said. “They were so mad about the Supreme Court decision.” 

Kupec was part of a DFL-controlled Legislature that then clarified and expanded abortion access in Minnesota. Peterson said at the candidate forum that he opposes abortion in most instances. 

Trump’s unpopularity notwithstanding, Peterson is a commercial real estate developer who believes he has a winning campaign message: Minnesotans are tired of new laws that add rigmarole and hidden costs to small businesses. 

It is a pitch he thinks will resonate because the District 4 borders North Dakota — a state with fewer rules around labor and starting a business, a topic that has inspired legislative ideas from Minnesota DFLers as well. 

“It’s really easy to set up a business in North Dakota,” Peterson said. 

Senator pothole 

Rob Kupec was a TV meteorologist at KVRR in Fargo who feared the consequences of a station ownership change.

“They gave me a lot of autonomy to present the weather the way I wanted to, to try new things, and I really valued that,” Kupec said at Black Cat Bakery in Moorhead. “And I thought if another company came in, there’s a good chance that it could go away.”

So Kupec fled before Coastal Television Broadcasting Group bought the Fox affiliate. He decided to run in a Senate district that included Fargo’s Minnesota sister city of Moorhead when incumbent Kent Eken announced his retirement in April 2022. 

“It was a midlife crisis,” joked Kupec, who said he and his wife moved to Moorhead 25 years ago. “Instead of a convertible, I ran for the state Senate. I have always been politically engaged and some of what I can do has been limited by being on television.” 

Kupec said he didn’t come to St. Paul with “some big agenda.”

During his time at the Capitol, he emphasized infrastructure investment, especially the “very unsexiness of lift stations” — pumps used to collect wastewater in order to stop floods. FEMA has designated Moorhead land near the Red River at a high enough flood risk that property owners must buy flood insurance.

Kupec said $10 million he secured in the state’s most recent bonding bill, plus a $10 million match from Moorhead-Fargo’s Metro Flood Diversion Authority, will enable the completion of a new lift station that will satisfy FEMA and remove the requirement to buy flood insurance.

On a leisurely drive across Moorhead, Kupec pointed to these and other infrastructure updates. For example, $4 million from the 2023 bonding bill went to a new fire station in the city of Dilworth, which abuts Moorhead to the east. 

(Our journey was marked by Kupec using his local knowledge to dodge being stalled by trains. He said that 80 trains each day cross a rail line currently operated by BNSF.) 

Kupec’s statewide initiatives included sponsoring the Digital Fair Repair Act, which went into effect in 2024. The law forces makers of products like smart phones to publicize enough information about said product so that people can make repairs without having to take it back to the manufacturer. 

Related: The walkover districts: Uncontested Minnesota Legislative races tilt strongly in DFL’s favor

The lawmaker noted that versions of the bill “had been languishing for years.” Advocates reached out to him to carry the measure after he cut a campaign commercial in favor of it.

“It was taking on Google and Apple and a lot of really big companies,” he said. 

Otherwise, Kupec emphasized that 70% of the bills he has introduced have a Republican co-sponsor. 

Chief among these is a measure with Senate Minority Leader Mark Johnson, R-East Grand Forks, that would expand tax reductions “in specific Minnesota cities located along the western border,” including Moorhead and East Grand Forks.

Kupec said border city businesses need these breaks in part because they have higher labor costs than their North Dakota counterparts. For example, the minimum wage in Minnesota is $11.41 an hour while it has remained at $7.25 an hour in North Dakota since 2009. 

And here is where Kupec and Peterson’s priorities converge — and yet also where Peterson says Kupec and the DFL are harmful. 

“We’re giving businesses too much of a reason to leave our state,” Austin Peterson said. 

Beyond the red tape

Peterson suggests meeting at his office building for an interview on his campaign. This wouldn’t be notable, except the building is in Fargo, North Dakota.

The choice was deliberate. As a real estate developer in Minnesota, North Dakota and South Dakota, he wanted to emphasize how subtle changes in proximity can belie vastly different regulatory landscapes.

“You didn’t feel the difference driving from downtown Moorhead to downtown Fargo, but there’s a tax difference,” he said. “There’s a business difference. Everything about it is different, and it’s geared to benefit North Dakota businesses, and it puts a crutch on Minnesota. So we have to get rid of that.”

Peterson’s property developments include a commercial business park and medical campus in Hawley. Rather than an “issues” tab on his website, he has a landing page for just one issue: economic development. 

Peterson repeated a phrase familiar by now to anyone following the Minnesota Republican Party: “unfunded mandates,” which means local governments, businesses, or individuals bearing the cost and compliance effort of new state rules.

Pressed for an example of these unfunded mandates, Peterson mentioned Paid Family and Medical Leave. 

The state program, which kicked off this January, requires businesses to let workers get paid up to 90% of their normal salary to take weeks off for major medical or caregiving life events. Its funding mechanism is a payroll tax that employees and employers both contribute toward.

Neither North nor South Dakota has paid leave. 

He says Kupec helped make it happen. 

“One of the deciding votes happened to be the senator in this district, and in my opinion he could have said, “Hey, let’s pause it. Let’s see what this could do,’” he said.

Related: Cows, colleges and competitive districts: DFL, GOP eye key House seats covering Northfield and St. Peter 

(At the candidate forum, Kupec said he was open to exploring revisions to the nascent program.)

Peterson, who is 40, hails from North Dakota but now calls the rural part of District 4 his home. He lives about 30 miles east of Moorhead in Rollag, which, if Googled, turns up a massive steam threshers festival, where people showcase oldfangled farm equipment used to separate grain. 

Unlike these steam-run machines, Peterson touts an “all gas, no brakes” campaign mantra. He bills himself as the proverbial high-energy, shaker-upper in the race, which voters can take or leave.

Growing up, Kupec glowed in Peterson’s living room as the area weather man. Most of his recollections of the television personality, however, are relatable to many Upper Midwest kids of a certain age: waiting for the chyron to tell him if school would be canceled.

Outside of his professional life, Peterson serves on his church board, the Hawley School Board and a little-known state board called the Minnesota Legislative Salary Council, which is tasked with recommending lawmaker salaries and per diem rates. 

Minnesota’s Supreme Court chief justice appointed Peterson to the council, which is required to be bipartisan. 

With that experience banked up, Peterson said he understands the importance of working across the aisle in a purple district.

“Just because I’m on the Republican platform doesn’t mean I can’t have a conversation with a Democrat and say how can we work together,” he said. “That’s what this district needs.”

Let’s play 29 questions

Peterson received a political baptism by fire at the League of Women Voters’ event where both candidates gave impromptu answers to 29 different questions posed by audience members. 

The queries ranged from whether to totally end the social security tax benefit (both candidates said ‘yes’) to the very issue tearing Minnesota apart: The increasing cost of registering a pontoon boat. 

(In all seriousness, the cost to register a pontoon boat varies depending on the length of the vessel. Both Peterson and Kupec answered this question by veering to the more familiar political ground of car tab fees, though Peterson said he would like to reexamine fees on all recreational vehicles. Kupec noted that pontoon boat fees are important revenue for the state, because they help fund the state Department of Natural Resources.)

On some subjects — such as gun control — Peterson clearly defined himself as a conservative.

Peterson said he would have voted ‘no’ against the gun control package Kupec helped pass in the Senate banning assault weapons, but he would have fought for the non-gun related school safety measures in the bill. 

Related: A Northfield farmer hopes to add a rare rural voice to the Minnesota Senate’s DFL caucus

But Peterson also distanced himself from Trump by stating his opposition to the U.S. invasion of Iran and the White House’s efforts to punish journalists and further restrict their access to decisionmakers and public records.

“Journalism is an important part of our society,” the Republican candidate. “Whether you like it or not, they have a duty to inform people.”

But on topics that veered away from economic development or hot-button issues, Peterson at times lost his footing.

For example, on ending Minnesota’s 32-year-old ban on nuclear power, Peterson said he would “explore all options” and spoke neither well nor poorly of nuclear power.

Kupec said he would like to end the ban. “We still don’t know what to do with nuclear waste,” he told the crowd. “But it is a good, clean, carbon free source of electricity.” 

Peterson was not the only one moving to the middle. Kupec took stances that may play better in Moorhead than Minneapolis, like joining Peterson in questioning legislation by state Rep. Aisha Gomez, DFL-Minneapolis, to levy a 1% tax on people with wealth assets of over $10 million. 

“We are one of the highest taxed states in the country,” Kupec said. “I would be very tepid on that proposal.”
news.summary:
State Sen. (and meteorologist) Rob Kupec and GOP challenger Austin Peterson are squaring off in the race to represent the Moorhead area in St. Paul.

AUDIE CORNISH: New polling from the New York Times over the weekend is showing that Republicans are on the defensive for five Senate seats. 

The polls show a lead for Democrats in states including Alaska, where they're up by seven points. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico is up by six, and it's a toss-up for Republican-held seats in Ohio, Kansas, and Iowa, and a leading issue is the economy. 

When likely voters in several battleground states were asked how Donald Trump is handling the economy, 61 percent say they disapprove. The White House isn't so sure. 

[Cuts to video]

KEVIN HASSETT: Ahead of an election cycle, the fact that there's, you know, possibly partisan pollsters telling us that the people are really, really depressed, it's a classic Democrat move, and I just don't buy it. 

[Cuts back to live]

CORNISH: Joining me now in the group chat, Sara Fischer, CNN senior media analyst and senior media reporter at Axios, Tiana Lowe Doescher, political commentator at the Washington Examiner, and Maria Cardona, CNN political commentator and Democratic strategist. Good morning, guys. Thank you so much for being here.

Sara, I want to start with you because what he said was very specific, that there are pollsters out there, that they're biased, that we shouldn't pay attention to these numbers.

And I realize, maybe the White House is thinking that that poll that was done in 2024 by the Des Moines Register in Iowa, that did have Kamala Harris up by a few points., and the, the White House even sued. But are they saying to themselves, well, that one was bad, so all the ones we've ever seen again are going to be bad?

SARA FISCHER: Yeah, but it's a strange thing to say to yourself, because at this point, whether or not you believe the polls is irrelevant. You have to figure out how you're going to win the state. And so just trying to dismiss the data as it is is not really practical.

I'm glad that you brought up the Des Moines case, because the pollster there, Ann Selzer, she was part of a lawsuit that the president waged against the Des Moines Register at the time, the pollster, Ann, and then the parent company to the Des Moines Register, USA Today, Inc. A judge actually tossed that suit and said, you can't just sue because you don't like polls.

And I kind of feel the same way, just looking at this as an outside analyst. You can't just look at polls and wag your finger and say, well, because the polls are biased, this is not the right data. Regardless of whether or not you think the data is biased or not, this is what people are making decisions on in terms of election spend.

CORNISH: And we hear him using the phrase "worried." We're worried about, we're worried about, which he rarely does.

I want to point to the ten Senate states that people are talking as toss-ups or potential to flip. And over the weekend, when I was doing my prep for, ahead of midterms, what did I notice? Lot of agriculture areas, lot of rural areas.

So, when we say that he was up by double digits the last time we won them, we mean it. And so I'm wondering if there is a reality check, that the diesel prices someone has to drive on in Iowa. Or the gas prices, or the tariffs someone has to deal with in Kansas and Georgia and Maine, that those, that's coming home to roost.

news.title: Democrats Are Struggling to Beat Susan Collins. You Can (Still) Blame One Man.
news.text:
Democrats hoping to retake the U.S. Senate have been enjoying a run of good luck. With Election Day barely four weeks away, polls show the party’s candidates leading in North Carolina, Georgia, and even Texas. Michigan, which looked iffy after a divisive primary that pitted centrists against progressives, seems increasingly winnable. Political forecasters have shifted races in deep-red Kansas and South Carolina toward Democrats, too, even though both remain long shots. And Donald Trump’s approval ratings continue to sink, creating formidable headwinds for any candidate with an R next to their name.

But then there’s Maine. In the Pine Tree State, Democratic former state Sen. Troy Jackson appears to be struggling in his bid to unseat longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins. A gold-standard poll last month found Collins leading Jackson by 3 points, triggering a mini-freakout among Democrats. Conducted by the New York Times and Siena University in partnership with the local Portland Press Herald newspaper, the survey was notably worse for Jackson than others taken before and since. But polls generally show a close race, a major letdown in a state that went for Kamala Harris by 7 points in 2024 and where the Democrat running for governor this year remains comfortably ahead. Collins is the only Republican senator up for reelection in a state that Harris won. That means a Jackson loss would hugely complicate Democrats’ path to reclaiming the Senate, forcing the party to bank on winning far more conservative states.

So what’s going on? Some blame Jackson’s lack of charisma and mealymouthed speaking style. Others say consultants have transformed his campaign into a Washington-run effort ill-suited to a political moment that favors outsiders. Still others point out that Collins has repeatedly managed to get reelected, Maine’s blue-state status be damned. And some think the Times/Siena/Press Herald poll may be off, making things look more dire for Jackson than they really are.

Yet if Jackson really is losing, it could also be because there’s a specter haunting his candidacy like something out of Stephen King. That specter is Graham Platner, Democrats’ original Senate nominee in Maine, whose gravel-voiced populist rhetoric caused national donors, progressive pundits, and 156,000 primary voters to swoon. Despite weathering a series of scandals—including revelations that he’d spouted offensive views on Reddit, gotten a Nazi tattoo as a drunken Marine, received significant financial support from his well-heeled father, and cheated on his wife shortly into their marriage—Platner was forced to drop out in July after an ex-girlfriend accused him of sexual assault. (He denies the allegations.)

Those scandals left Maine Democrats with little choice but to replace Platner on the ballot. After holding meetings around the state at which voters nominated delegates, the party overwhelmingly picked Jackson at a statewide convention in late July. But swapping candidates didn’t erase the coalition that chose Platner in the first place, and did so with the most votes any Democratic Senate primary candidate in Maine has ever gotten. That fact has locked Jackson into a contest shaped in his predecessor’s mold, giving him the unenviable task of beating a resilient incumbent from a standing start with someone else’s playbook.

Platner’s catastrophic candidacy continues to shadow Jackson in multiple ways. For one thing, the two-and-a-half-week scramble to replace him left Jackson with a shorter runway to make the case against Collins, whose nearly three decades in office have made her a ubiquitous figure. A former president of the Maine state Senate, Jackson ran for governor this year and finished third in the first round of the June primary, despite endorsements from Platner and Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders. Yet in the Times/Siena/Press Herald poll, fully 10 percent of likely Maine voters said they hadn’t heard of Jackson or didn’t know enough to have an opinion about him, nearly seven times the number who said so of Collins.

Simply having to replace someone else may also be putting Jackson behind. History suggests that voters generally don’t look kindly on candidate switcheroos. It can make the previous nominee’s supporters feel cheated and invite charges that his replacement lacks a genuine democratic mandate. Perhaps for that reason, such swap-outs rarely happen and succeed even less often. According to the Times, the major parties have replaced Senate nominees in just nine races over the past three decades, and in only two of those cases did the replacement candidate go on to win the general election. It probably didn’t help that Platner’s exit from the race was maximally bridge-burning. Bucking advisers’ entreaties, he released an 11-minute video in which he accused a “corporate media system and the political establishment” of acting “as judge, jury and executioner” to force him out.

Platner’s transgressions have also created political dilemmas for Jackson, who repeatedly vouched for the oysterman’s character until the rape allegation ended his campaign. “I know there’s a lot of people in here that were campaigning for Graham,” Jackson told voters in August. “I wish none of this would’ve happened like this.” New York magazine reports that Democratic consultants’ efforts to separate Jackson from Platner—including advising their candidate not to say Platner’s name—have alienated many of the volunteers who originally latched onto Platner’s candidacy. But at the same time, two-thirds of Maine voters in the Times survey had an unfavorable view of Platner, about the same share who disapproved of Trump. Jackson has attacked Collins for failing to strongly oppose the president, but here he is talking wistfully about someone who’s about as unpopular.

The association has left Jackson vulnerable from the right, too. Collins-aligned ads have also sought to play up their connections; one showed footage of Jackson and Platner greeting one another like bros while campaigning. Yet disowning Platner entirely doesn’t appear to be an option, either. The on-the-fly delegate system the Maine Democratic Party devised to replace Platner seems to have left some liberal voters skeptical of Jackson unless he hews closely to his predecessor’s politics. “Why should frustrated Mainers like me trust you as the person to take over leadership of that movement?” one voter recently asked Jackson, referring to Platner’s campaign.

As that question suggests, ideology may be another way in which Platner’s ghost is haunting Jackson’s chances. Maine Democrats rallied around Jackson despite having other candidates to choose from in part because he seemed like the most natural heir to Platner’s progressive platform. Both support Medicare for All, taxing billionaires, and cutting off U.S. military aid to Israel. Yet even when Platner was running, it was far from clear that full-throated progressivism was the best path to beating Collins. She cruised to victory in 2020 thanks in part to a sizable chunk of suburban women who split their tickets between her and Joe Biden. Some self-identified Democrats who told the Times that they planned to vote for Collins this year cited her moderate reputation, and more Mainers viewed Jackson as extreme than saw Collins that way.

Which leads to what may be the biggest albatross Platner has thrown over the race: his example. Despite all his flaws, Platner rose from political obscurity to become his party’s nominee for Senate in less than a year, earning national headlines while handily beating Maine’s sitting governor and other candidates. He’s a gifted communicator who inspired enormous loyalty among rank-and-file voters and impressed longtime Democratic operatives, some of whom hailed him as the next coming of Barack Obama. Along the way, Platner and his advisers laid out a theory for how to finally beat Collins: an unabashedly economic populism articulated by a political outsider whose masculine workingman’s affect would win back the kinds of voters who have abandoned Democrats in the Trump era.

Before he dropped out, there were signs that even Platner might not have been able to deliver on that lofty vision. In a Times/Siena/Press Herald poll from June, Platner was polling about as well with white working-class Mainers as had Sara Gideon, the establishment-backed Democrat who lost to Collins in 2020. Perhaps for that reason, some of Jackson’s advisers seem to be pushing him in a different direction. Yet precisely because Platner is no longer around to test it, his theory of the race continues to beckon other Maine Democrats like a siren call. So now the party is stuck, trying to win an election Platner shaped with a candidate who has to shoulder much of his predecessor’s baggage but lacks many of his talents.

Democrats’ dreams of winning back the Senate may end up being the biggest casualty of that bitter inheritance. Of course, it’s true that Jackson’s team has also made some questionable choices about how to deploy their candidate of late. Last week, an ad that inexplicably showed Jackson sipping boba tea while criticizing Collins’ ties to “the one-percenters” drew online derision. Jackson has baggage all his own, too. While serving in the Maine senate, he reportedly yelled at a female colleague and threw a plastic water bottle in anger during a dispute over a bill. Jackson is also in a long-term relationship with his second cousin, with whom he has two children. In the latest Times poll, Jackson’s approval ratings are underwater, slightly below where Platner’s were about a week before he dropped out. Fully 12 percent of 2024 Harris voters say they plan to cast a ballot for Collins, compared to just 3 percent of 2024 Trump voters who back Jackson.

Had Platner stayed in, he might well have gone on to lose. And it’s certainly still possible that Jackson will overcome these deficits to win. But in politics, few things are more tempting than the road not taken.
news.summary: In a year that’s shaping up so well for Democrats, things still look dicey in Maine.

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed and Elissa Slotkin have their differences — and argue their common ground is more important
news.text:
WARREN, Mich. — If Democrat Abdul El-Sayed pulls off a win next month in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race, he and the state’s senior senator — Elissa Slotkin — will make a unique duo.

The two Democrats will both have defeated the same Republican opponent — Mike Rogers — to get the job. They will both be among the youngest lawmakers in the chamber. And they may very well be, as Slotkin has said, the youngest state delegation in the Senate come next year.

They also will share some notable differences.

El-Sayed is a Muslim man, and Slotkin is a Jewish woman — a distinction that has taken on particular significance given the number of column inches that have been spent focusing on El-Sayed’s views on Israel and Middle East politics.

In an exclusive joint interview with MS NOW this weekend, just moments after the pair wrapped up their first joint appearance of the campaign, El-Sayed and Slotkin touted their different faith backgrounds and foreign policy beliefs as “good for Michigan.”

El-Sayed said he looks forward to being able “to demonstrate that you can have deeply held disagreements and still choose to fight together on the deeply held points of agreement.”

“That is a choice, and that’s a choice that people in Michigan have been making for a very long time,” he said. “It’s exciting that we might be able to model that at the level of the United States senate.”

Slotkin agreed, telling MS NOW that “people want to see a Jewish woman and a Muslim man being able to get along, debate, push and pull on each other, and move the state forward.”

“It may be even important internationally for the world to see that we can actually get along, even though there are things where we really disagree on,” she added.

MS NOW spoke with El-Sayed and Slotkin on Saturday following their appearance at an hourlong town hall that drew hundreds of voters, local politicians and activists.

The location of the gathering — especially given that it was their first joint event — was notable in and of itself: a union hall in bellwether Macomb County.

Two years ago, Slotkin’s performance in Macomb helped propel her to victory in her Senate race despite President Donald Trump winning Michigan on the same night.

Slotkin outperformed Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris in the county, losing by approximately 9 points compared to Harris’ 14 point loss to Trump.

“Macomb County is going to be absolutely critical,” El-Sayed told the crowd on Saturday.

Of course, a boost from Slotkin here could help.

Waiting in line to enter the town hall, Macomb County voter Christina Jolly told MS NOW that having Slotkin on the trail with El-Sayed “means a lot,” arguing it could serve as a reassurance to those who may be on the fence about the Democratic nominee.

“You have different beliefs where they do disagree, but they agree on what's important for America,” Jolly said. 

During the event, El-Sayed and Slotkin echoed that theme — telling the crowd that just because they did not agree on every policy prescription for the country’s problems (see: healthcare) or foreign policy didn’t mean they disagreed on the things they considered “really important.”

The duo fielded questions on what they will do to fight corruption in government, how they will stand up for union workers and what they will do to protect public education.

Throughout the event, they both cast themselves as fighters — eager to tackle rising costs, defend the middle class and take on Trump’s alleged corruption.

“I am on Team Fight,” Slotkin told the crowd. Pointing at El-Sayed, she added, “And I need someone with me who is on Team Fight.”

The question remains, however, what such “fighters” can actually get done in Washington. Even if Democrats manage to wrest control of both chambers in November, Trump will still have his veto pen.

Asked what’s reasonable to expect a Democrat-controlled Congress to actually accomplish in that environment — beyond oversight of the executive branch — the duo pointed to issues like addressing artificial intelligence and food safety.

Slotkin invoked the grassroots pressure around artificial intelligence, casting it as an issue that has “bubbled right up to the House and the Senate” in recent months and that is not necessarily “Democrat versus Republican.”

El-Sayed — who leaned on his past work in public health to rail against recent food recalls, including notably of lettuce — argued that “existential” issues “should be easy to get done” given the public outcry from the American public.

“The idea that we should be dodging lettuce in the United States of America is nuts,” he told MS NOW. 

At the same time, though, both did not discount the potential political benefit if Democrats have their agenda blocked by Trump. Both agreed it would be wise for the party to pass legislation fulfilling their campaign promises — such as addressing the cost of living — and “dare” Trump to veto or ignore it.

“Challenging Donald Trump to vote against a housing bill or to vote against something that makes people have a better quality of life,” Slotkin said, “dare him to do that in front of the American public.”

Both El-Sayed and Slotkin have made a point on the campaign to talk about ushering a new generation of Democrats into office.

Speaking with MS NOW, Slotkin suggested her call for change has more to do with tactics than any internecine left versus moderate standoff within the party.

Some of her current colleagues, she said, “grew up in a Senate that I have never seen or experienced.”

“I’m interested in people across the political spectrum who are interested in a new approach to exerting oversight and power,” she said.

El-Sayed echoed that tactical argument, pointing to social media and how short clips online can help craft the political narrative.

“You think about how the Senate operates, it is quite clear that the body does not fully take seriously that information moves by way of the internet and clips,” he said. 

“There is an opportunity for us to upgrade not just our tactics, but also an understanding of strategy about what conversation we ought to have,” El-Sayed added. “Democracy is not just a conversation between 100 senators. Democracy is a conversation between all of us and the 350 million people who elect all of us.”

MS NOW’s interview with El-Sayed and Slotkin came as polling shows that the race between El-Sayed and Rogers remains neck-and-neck.

A recent Fox News poll put El-Sayed ahead by only 1 point among likely voters. Other surveys have El-Sayed with a slightly larger lead but still within the margin of error.

At the same time, in other redder pockets of the country — such as Texas, Alaska and even Kansas — Democrats are making major inroads in the polls.

If Democrats are seeing the tide rising in these Trump-friendly areas, then why isn’t the race in Michigan less of a nail-biter?

El-Sayed told MS NOW that it’s because of the “deep money disadvantage” that he’s facing as Republican groups pour money into the state.

He also pointed to how Republicans have sought to make El-Sayed a bogeyman well beyond Michigan’s borders.

“JD Vance literally told all of the Republicans to just run against me,” El-Sayed said. “They want to distract some of the issues on which this election is going to really hinge: the price of gas, the price of groceries. Can you see a doctor?”

For her part, Slotkin predicted that the Midwest could be “the story” of election night. 

Arguing voters in the Midwest tend to be “very practical, reasonable people,” Slotkin told MS NOW that folks here are “absolutely fed up with the failure of Donald Trump to do the one thing he said he was going to do, which is put money in the pocket.”

Saturday’s town hall may have been Slotkin’s first campaign stop alongside El-Sayed, but it was hardly her first time on the trail this cycle.Outside of Michigan, Slotkin has campaigned for Democrats over the past year in places such as Iowa, Ohio and Pennsylvania — states that are, notably, traditional presidential battlegrounds. She is also set to headline a fundraiser in Nevada in the coming days.

Asked about 2028 and a potential presidential bid, Slotkin didn’t count herself out of the running, but she declined to show her cards.

Explaining her campaign travel, she returned to her “next generation” pitch, telling MS NOW, “I just want to be a part of that next generation that's going to do big things in the country.”

“Whether it’s me, someone else,” she said, “that new generation and kind of shepherding in that new — I want to be part of that.”

If things go Democrats’ way in a month, El-Sayed could be one part of that new generation.

news.title: The IRGC’s Midterm Endorsement Creates a Problem for Democrats
news.text:
The Democrats are in a quandary. They’re perplexed by a problem of their own making.

How can they deal with an endorsement from the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps calling on Americans to vote for Democratic candidates in the November mid-terms? This is too delicious. I wish I had made it up, but I didn’t. 

I’ve lost count of the War Powers Resolution bills that the Dems have offered to end the Iran war abruptly. They have all failed — not because Americans recognize the legitimacy of the war against Iran’s nuclear weapons — but because Republicans have managed so far to kill the bills.

Kamala Harris is among the presidential contenders who oppose the Iran war. In Illinois, Lt. Gov. Juliana Stratton and U.S. Rep. Robin Kelly — contenders to succeed Sen. Dick Durbin — have both promised to vote against further funding for the Iran war.

Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said he didn’t want to comment on Ayatollah Khamenei’s death because “there are a lot of people in Dearborn who are sad today.” When confronted by a student whose family was persecuted by the Tehran regime, El-Sayed responded by arguing that the United States has too often acted as “the world’s policeman” while saying he supported movements for democracy and freedom abroad. As if there is any democracy or freedom in Iran.

Rep. Raja Krishnamoorti (D-Chicago) said the war was illegal and unconstitutional.

On September 29, the IRGC sent a very long letter to the American people urging them to vote against any candidates backed by President Trump because he and Israel were the cause of the war. The letter also claimed that the Iranian nuclear program was entirely peaceful and that the IRGC was not a terrorist group, writing that there was not, “a single verifiable instance where the IRGC has committed an act of violence against civilians.”

The IRGC has been the principal terrorist arm of the Tehran regime. It controls Iran’s ballistic missiles and its terrorist proxy forces such as Hamas and Hizballah. They are responsible for Iran’s attacks on oil tankers and much more.

The IRGC are the first to line up to chant “death to America” and to force others to chant the same. The IRGC has committed thousands of murders of Iranian civilians as well as attempted assassinations of dissidents in other countries. The Iranian nuclear program has even been condemned by the UN’s International Atomic Energy Agency for enriching uranium far beyond what would be required for a nuclear power plant.

So what can the Democrats do? They cannot go against their candidates who speak out in favor of Iran so they — the national “leaders” of the Party — remain silent.

But who are the Democrats’ leaders? California Gov. Gavin Newsome has ripped Mr. Trump on the Iran war. Former vice president Kamala Harris has done the same.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt) has condemned the war as illegal and unconstitutional as has Rep. Alexandria Ocasio Cortez (D-NY). Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker (D) has condemned the war saying it was “illegal” and demanded that the troops be brought home. If there are other “leaders” of the Democratic Party they have remained silent.

These remarks are conclusive evidence — given the silence of other Dems — that the Democrats support Iran and not America.

As long as the Democratic leaders remain content with their condemnations of the Iran war there is no element of sanity in the Democrats. They are rabid in their opposition to Mr. Trump and offer no solutions to the war other than ending it.

It should be enough for the American voters to see that the Democrats have nothing more than condemnation of Mr. Trump and to vote for the candidates Mr. Trump backs. It won’t be. Mr. Trump is in the fight of his life in the mid-terms. If he doesn’t win across the board — keeping the House and the Senate — he will be a very lonely guy. He will be impeached again and will have to oppose more War Powers resolutions on the Iran war that seek to end it abruptly. And he may lose one of those votes. 

The president has said that the war in Iran will be over shortly after the mid-terms. But how can it be? If we don’t destroy the Iranian regime they will, certainly, go back to their pursuit of nuclear weapons. They will continue to sponsor terrorism around the world.

It should be enough for the American voters to see the Democrats in an act of ultimate disloyalty. But, as this column has already said, it will not be. The Iran war is a distant concern to them. They are concerned with what Joe Biden used to call “kitchen table” issues such as the price of gasoline and food, the flow of which will be slowed — and grow more expensive — by the price of diesel fuel.

If the American voter is more concerned with those issues than with the Iran war Mr. Trump will lose the mid-terms and be isolated politically. They may vote exactly how the IRGC said they should.
